\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION A \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Mathematical and Quantum Foundations \hfill Q.1--20\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{1}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Density matrix of a pure state}
The density matrix of the pure state $\ket\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + i\ket1)$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & -i\\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & i\\ -i & 1\end{pmatrix}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & -i\\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} A pure state's density matrix is the outer product $\ket\psi\!\bra\psi$; the bra is the conjugate transpose of the ket.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho_{ij} = \psi_i\psi_j^*$; for $\alpha\ket0 + \beta\ket1$: $\rho = \begin{psmallmatrix}|\alpha|^2 & \alpha\beta^*\\ \alpha^*\beta & |\beta|^2\end{psmallmatrix}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\rho = \ket\psi\!\bra\psi$ with $\ket\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ i\end{pmatrix}$ and $\bra\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,\ -i)$ (complex conjugate
transpose). Hence $\rho = \frac12\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot1 & 1\cdot(-i)\\ i\cdot1 & i\cdot(-i)\end{pmatrix} = \frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & -i\\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
\emph{Check}: Hermitian, trace 1, $\rho^2 = \rho$ (pure). Its Bloch vector is $(0, 1, 0)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $I/2$ is the maximally mixed state; a pure state has $\rho^2 = \rho$ and non-zero coherence here.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This is $\ket+\!\bra+$; the relative phase $i$ must appear in the off-diagonal elements.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This forgets the complex conjugate in the bra: it is the density matrix of $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 - i\ket1)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $\rho_{01} = \alpha\beta^*$: phases live in the off-diagonal elements.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{2}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$}
The purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ of $\rho = \begin{pmatrix}0.7 & 0.3\\ 0.3 & 0.3\end{pmatrix}$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.58$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.76$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.52$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.76$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ distinguishes pure (1) from mixed ($<1$) states; it equals the sum of squared moduli of all entries.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \sum_{ij}|\rho_{ij}|^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$ for a qubit.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \sum_{ij}|\rho_{ij}|^2 = 0.7^2 + 0.3^2 + 0.3^2 + 0.3^2 = 0.49 + 0.09 + 0.09 + 0.09 = 0.76$.
\emph{Check} with the Bloch vector: $x = 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{01} = 0.6$, $z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11} = 0.4$, $|\vec r|^2 = 0.52$ and
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2} = 0.76$. Since $0.76 < 1$ the state is mixed.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.58$ keeps only the diagonal ($0.49 + 0.09$) and forgets both off-diagonal terms.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1$ would mean a pure state, but $\det\rho = 0.12 \neq 0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.52$ is $|\vec r|^2$, not the purity $\frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Purity = sum of $|\rho_{ij}|^2$; the off-diagonals count twice.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{3}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Bloch vector from $\rho$}
The Bloch vector $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ of $\rho = \begin{pmatrix}0.8 & 0.2 - 0.1i\\ 0.2 + 0.1i & 0.2\end{pmatrix}$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$(0.2,\ 0.1,\ 0.6)$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$(0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.6)$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$(0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.6)$ & \optlabel{D}\,$(0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.8)$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $(0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.6)$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Every qubit density matrix is $\frac12(I + \vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$; the Bloch vector components are Pauli expectation values.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $r_x = 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{10}$, $r_y = 2\operatorname{Im}\rho_{10}$, $r_z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$; $\rho_{01} = \frac{r_x - ir_y}{2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Write $\rho = \frac12(I + r_xX + r_yY + r_zZ) = \frac12\begin{pmatrix}1 + r_z & r_x - ir_y\\ r_x + ir_y & 1 - r_z\end{pmatrix}$.
Then $r_z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11} = 0.6$, and $\rho_{10} = \frac12(r_x + ir_y) = 0.2 + 0.1i$ gives $r_x = 0.4$, $r_y = 0.2$.
Equivalently $r_k = \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_k)$. $|\vec r|^2 = 0.56 < 1$: a valid mixed state.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This forgets the factor 2 between off-diagonal entries and Bloch components.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The sign of $r_y$ is read from $\rho_{01}$ instead of $\rho_{10}$: $\rho_{01} = \frac{r_x - ir_y}{2}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $r_z = 0.8$ uses $\rho_{00}$ instead of $\rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $\vec r = (\operatorname{Tr}\rho X, \operatorname{Tr}\rho Y, \operatorname{Tr}\rho Z)$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{4}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Validity of density matrices}
Which of the following matrices is \emph{not} a valid density matrix?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.5 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.5 & -0.3i\\ 0.3i & 0.5\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.9 & 0\\ 0 & 0.1\end{pmatrix}$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.6 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & 0.4\end{pmatrix}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\begin{pmatrix}0.6 & 0.5\\ 0.5 & 0.4\end{pmatrix}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Valid density matrices: Hermitian, unit trace, positive semi-definite (non-negative eigenvalues).

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} For $2\times2$ Hermitian matrices with trace 1: PSD $\Leftrightarrow \det\rho \ge 0 \Leftrightarrow |\vec r| \le 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} A density matrix must be Hermitian, have trace 1 and be positive semi-definite. All four are Hermitian with trace 1; for a
$2\times2$ matrix PSD $\Leftrightarrow$ $\det\rho \ge 0$. $\det\begin{psmallmatrix}0.6&0.5\\0.5&0.4\end{psmallmatrix} = 0.24 - 0.25 = -0.01 < 0$:
one eigenvalue is negative (a ``probability'' below zero). The others have determinants $0$ (pure $\ket+$), $0.09$ and $0.25 - 0.09 = 0.16$.
Equivalently the Bloch vector of the first has length $\sqrt{1^2 + 0.2^2} > 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\ket+\!\bra+$: $\det = 0$, eigenvalues 1 and 0, a valid pure state.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\det = 0.25 - 0.09 = 0.16 > 0$; eigenvalues $0.8$ and $0.2$: valid.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] A diagonal matrix with entries $0.9, 0.1$ is a valid mixed state.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Check the determinant (or $|\vec r| \le 1$), not just trace and Hermiticity.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{5}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Trace preservation of Kraus sets}
The operators $K_0 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$ and $K_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0 & b\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ ($b \ge 0$) form a
trace-preserving set of Kraus operators exactly when $b$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.6$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.36$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.8$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.4$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.6$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Kraus operators of a channel must satisfy the completeness (trace-preservation) relation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\sum_kK_k^\dagger K_k = I$; amplitude damping $K_0 = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sqrt{1-\gamma})$, $K_1 = \sqrt\gamma\ket0\!\bra1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Trace preservation requires $\sum_kK_k^\dagger K_k = I$. $K_0^\dagger K_0 = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.64)$ and
$K_1^\dagger K_1 = \begin{psmallmatrix}0&0\\b&0\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}0&b\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix} = \operatorname{diag}(0, b^2)$.
So $0.64 + b^2 = 1$, $b = 0.6$. This is amplitude damping with $\gamma = 0.36$: $K_0 = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sqrt{1-\gamma})$, $K_1 = \sqrt\gamma\ket0\!\bra1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $b^2 = 0.36$ is required, so $b = 0.6$; choosing $b = 0.36$ confuses $b$ with $b^2$ and gives $0.64 + 0.13 = 0.77 \neq 1$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $b = 0.8$ gives $K_0^\dagger K_0 + K_1^\dagger K_1 = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.64 + 0.64) = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1.28)$: probability would be created.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $b = 0.4$ gives $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0.64 + 0.16) = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.80)$: 20\,\% of the $\ket1$ population would disappear.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Completeness: $K_0^\dagger K_0 + K_1^\dagger K_1 = I$ fixes $b^2 = 1 - 0.64$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{6}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Random phases $\to$ dephasing}
A qubit is prepared in $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + e^{i\varphi}\ket1)$ where the phase $\varphi$ is random and uniformly distributed in
$[-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2]$. The average value of $\langle X\rangle$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\pi/4 \approx 0.79$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1/2$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$2/\pi \approx 0.64$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $2/\pi \approx 0.64$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Averaging over a random phase reduces coherence: the origin of dephasing.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\langle X\rangle = \cos\varphi$; $\mathbb E\cos\varphi = \frac{1}{2\Delta}\int_{-\Delta}^{\Delta}\cos\varphi\,d\varphi = \frac{\sin\Delta}{\Delta}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For fixed $\varphi$, $\langle X\rangle = 2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha^*\beta) = \cos\varphi$. Averaging over the uniform distribution:
$\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\varphi\,d\varphi = \frac{1}{\pi}[\sin\varphi]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} = \frac2\pi \approx 0.637$.
The averaged state $\bar\rho$ has its off-diagonal element reduced from $\frac12$ to $\frac1\pi$: random phases are the origin of
\emph{dephasing}. Populations ($\langle Z\rangle = 0$) are unchanged.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\frac\pi4$ is the inverse of the correct ratio ($\frac{\Delta}{\sin\Delta}$ instead of $\frac{\sin\Delta}{\Delta}$ with $\Delta = \frac\pi2$) and exceeds the correct value.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\frac12$ is not the mean of $\cos\varphi$ on $[-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2]$; it would be the mean of $\cos^2\varphi$ (the average of $P(+)$-like quantities), not of $\langle X\rangle$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0$ would require the phase to be uniform over the whole circle $[-\pi, \pi]$, where positive and negative $\cos\varphi$ cancel; here $\cos\varphi \ge 0$ throughout.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Random phases shrink $\langle X\rangle$, not the populations.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{7}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Error-free probability $(1-p)^n$}
A circuit has 20 gates; each fails independently with probability $p = 0.01$. The probability that \emph{at least one} gate fails is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.182$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.818$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.200$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.165$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.182$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Independent failures; complement rule.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P(\ge1) = 1 - (1-p)^n$; $P(\text{exactly }k) = \binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $P(\text{no failure}) = (1 - p)^{20} = 0.99^{20} = e^{20\ln0.99} = e^{-0.2010} = 0.818$. Hence
$P(\ge1) = 1 - 0.818 = 0.182$. The linear estimate $20p = 0.200$ over-counts runs with two or more failures;
$P(\text{exactly one}) = 20(0.01)(0.99)^{19} = 0.165$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.818$ is the probability of \emph{no} failure.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $np = 0.2$ is a first-order approximation that over-counts.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.165$ is the probability of exactly one failure.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Error-free probability $(1-p)^G$ --- the notebook's lower bound.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{8}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Shot-noise standard error}
An outcome has true probability $0.9$. It is estimated from $10\,000$ shots. The standard error of the estimate is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.03$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.003$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.0009$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.009$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.003$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Binomial sampling error of an estimated probability.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{P(1-P)/S}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The count is binomial; the estimated frequency has $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{P(1 - P)/S} = \sqrt{0.9\cdot0.1/10\,000} = \sqrt{9\times10^{-6}} = 0.003$.
Shot noise is a \emph{statistical} error of the estimate, not a property of the quantum state: it shrinks like $1/\sqrt S$ even on a noiseless simulator.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.03 = \sqrt{0.09/100}$ is the standard error for only 100 shots; with $10^4$ shots it is ten times smaller.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.0009 = \frac{0.09}{100}$ is neither the variance $9\times10^{-6}$ nor its square root $0.003$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.009$ omits the square root: $\frac{0.9\times0.1}{10} = 0.009$ mixes the variance with a wrong divisor.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Shot noise $\propto 1/\sqrt S$: 10\,000 shots give $\pm0.003$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{9}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Coherent angle error}
An $X$ gate is implemented as $R_X(\pi + \varepsilon)$ instead of $R_X(\pi)$, with $\varepsilon = 0.1$ rad. Applied to $\ket0$, the
probability of measuring $0$ (an error) is closest to
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.0025$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.01$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.1$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.05$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.0025$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Rotation gates and coherent angle errors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $R_X(\theta) = \cos\frac\theta2I - i\sin\frac\theta2X$; $P(0) = \cos^2\frac{\pi + \varepsilon}{2} = \sin^2\frac\varepsilon2 \approx \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $R_X(\theta)\ket0 = \cos\frac\theta2\ket0 - i\sin\frac\theta2\ket1$, so $P(0) = \cos^2\frac{\pi + \varepsilon}{2} = \sin^2\frac\varepsilon2$.
For $\varepsilon = 0.1$: $\sin^2(0.05) = 0.0025$. A small \emph{coherent} angle error gives an error probability quadratic in $\varepsilon$
(but such errors add up in amplitude when repeated --- see Section D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.01 = \varepsilon^2$ forgets the half angle.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.1 = \varepsilon$ treats the angle as a probability.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.05 = \varepsilon/2$ is an amplitude, not a probability.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} A coherent error $\varepsilon$ costs $\approx\varepsilon^2/4$ in probability per gate.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{10}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Fidelity with a mixed state}
The fidelity $F = \braket{+|\rho|+}$ between the target $\ket+$ and the mixed state $\rho = 0.8\ket+\!\bra+ + 0.2\,\frac I2$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.6$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.9$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.8$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.95$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.9$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fidelity of a mixed state with a pure target is a linear function of $\rho$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $F = \braket{\psi|\rho|\psi}$; $\braket{\psi|\frac I2|\psi} = \frac12$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} By linearity, $\braket{+|\rho|+} = 0.8\braket{+|+}\braket{+|+} + 0.2\cdot\frac12\braket{+|+} = 0.8 + 0.1 = 0.9$.
The maximally mixed part still overlaps the target with probability $\frac12$. (For a pure target, $F = \braket{\psi|\rho|\psi}$; some texts use the square root.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.6$ subtracts the noisy part instead of adding its overlap.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.8$ ignores that the mixed part still overlaps the target.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.95 \approx \sqrt{0.9}$ is the root fidelity convention.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $F = (1-q) + q/d$ for a target mixed with white noise.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{11}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Partial trace; entanglement and mixedness}
For the two-qubit state $\ket\psi = \sqrt{0.8}\ket{00} + \sqrt{0.2}\ket{11}$, the purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2$ of the reduced state of qubit A is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.8$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.5$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.68$ & \optlabel{D}\,$1$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.68$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Partial trace; entanglement makes subsystems mixed.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\ket\psi\!\bra\psi$; for $\sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ket{ii}$: $\rho_A = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\rho_A = \operatorname{Tr}_B\ket\psi\!\bra\psi = 0.8\ket0\!\bra0 + 0.2\ket1\!\bra1$ (the cross terms $\ket{00}\!\bra{11}$ have orthogonal B parts and vanish).
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2 = 0.64 + 0.04 = 0.68$. The global state is pure, but its parts are mixed because they are entangled ---
the same mechanism by which a qubit entangled with its environment decoheres.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.8$ is the population $\rho_{A,00}$, not the purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2 = 0.8^2 + 0.2^2$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\frac12$ is the purity for the maximally entangled state $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$, where $\rho_A = \frac I2$; here the weights are $0.8$ and $0.2$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $1$ would hold for a product state such as $\ket{00}$; entanglement with qubit B makes $\rho_A$ mixed even though the global state is pure.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Decoherence = entanglement with an environment we trace out.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{12}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Eigenvalues of a qubit $\rho$}
The larger eigenvalue of $\rho = \begin{pmatrix}0.7 & 0.3\\ 0.3 & 0.3\end{pmatrix}$ is closest to
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.700$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.861$ & \optlabel{C}\,$1.000$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.760$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.861$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Eigenvalues of a qubit density matrix from its Bloch length.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda_\pm = \frac{1 \pm |\vec r|}{2}$; $\lambda_+\lambda_- = \det\rho$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For a qubit, $\lambda_\pm = \frac{1 \pm |\vec r|}{2}$. Here $\vec r = (0.6, 0, 0.4)$, $|\vec r| = \sqrt{0.52} = 0.7211$, so
$\lambda_+ = 0.8606$, $\lambda_- = 0.1394$. \emph{Check}: $\lambda_+ + \lambda_- = 1 = \operatorname{Tr}\rho$ and $\lambda_+\lambda_- = 0.12 = \det\rho = 0.21 - 0.09$;
$\lambda_+^2 + \lambda_-^2 = 0.76 = \operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.700$ is the diagonal entry $\rho_{00}$; diagonal entries equal eigenvalues only when the off-diagonal elements vanish, and here $\rho_{01} = 0.3$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] An eigenvalue $1$ would make the other eigenvalue $0$ and the state pure, but $\det\rho = 0.12 \neq 0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.760$ is the purity $\lambda_+^2 + \lambda_-^2$, not an eigenvalue.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Diagonal entries are not eigenvalues unless the coherence is zero.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{13}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Independent qubits: tensor product}
Two independent qubits are in the states $\rho_A = \operatorname{diag}(0.9, 0.1)$ and $\rho_B = \operatorname{diag}(0.8, 0.2)$. In the
state $\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$, the probability that both qubits give the \emph{same} outcome is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.74$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.50$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.26$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.72$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.74$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Product states of independent qubits; tensor products of diagonal matrices.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P(ab) = P_A(a)P_B(b)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\rho_A\otimes\rho_B = \operatorname{diag}(0.9\cdot0.8,\ 0.9\cdot0.2,\ 0.1\cdot0.8,\ 0.1\cdot0.2) = \operatorname{diag}(0.72, 0.18, 0.08, 0.02)$
in the order $\ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11}$. Same outcome: $0.72 + 0.02 = 0.74$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.5$ would hold for unbiased qubits; both qubits are strongly biased towards $0$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.26 = 0.18 + 0.08$ is the probability of \emph{different} outcomes ($01$ or $10$), the complement of the answer.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.72$ counts only the outcome $00$; the outcome $11$ (probability $0.1\times0.2 = 0.02$) also has both qubits equal.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Independent noise multiplies probabilities.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{14}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Conjugation $X\rho X$ on the Bloch sphere}
A qubit with Bloch vector $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ is acted on by $\rho \mapsto X\rho X$. Its new Bloch vector is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$(-r_x,\ -r_y,\ -r_z)$ & \optlabel{B}\,$(-r_x,\ r_y,\ r_z)$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$(r_x,\ -r_y,\ -r_z)$ & \optlabel{D}\,$(r_x,\ r_y,\ -r_z)$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $(r_x,\ -r_y,\ -r_z)$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Conjugation by a Pauli is a $\pi$ rotation of the Bloch sphere.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $XXX = X$, $XYX = -Y$, $XZX = -Z$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $X\rho X = \frac12(I + r_xXXX + r_yXYX + r_zXZX)$. Since $X$ commutes with itself and anticommutes with $Y$ and $Z$:
$XXX = X$, $XYX = -Y$, $XZX = -Z$. So $(r_x, r_y, r_z) \mapsto (r_x, -r_y, -r_z)$: a rotation by $\pi$ about the $x$-axis.
The bit-flip channel $(1 - p)\rho + pX\rho X$ therefore keeps $r_x$ and multiplies $r_y, r_z$ by $1 - 2p$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Inverting all three components is not a rotation (not a unitary map).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] This is conjugation by $Z$ or by a rotation about another axis, not by $X$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Only $r_z$ flipped would be a reflection, not a unitary rotation.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $X\rho X$: keep $r_x$, flip $r_y$, $r_z$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{15}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Bloch vectors of states}
Match each state (List-I) with its Bloch vector (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\ket1$ & \textbf{(1)} & $(0,\ 0,\ 0.5)$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $\frac I2$ & \textbf{(2)} & $(0,\ 0,\ 0)$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & $\frac12\begin{psmallmatrix}1 & -i\\ i & 1\end{psmallmatrix}$ & \textbf{(3)} & $(0,\ 0,\ -1)$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $\operatorname{diag}(0.75,\ 0.25)$ & \textbf{(4)} & $(0,\ 1,\ 0)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$4 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$1, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$3 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Bloch vectors of pure, mixed and maximally mixed states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $r_z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$, $r_x + ir_y = 2\rho_{10}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Use $r_z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$, $r_x + ir_y = 2\rho_{10}$.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item $\ket1$: south pole $(0, 0, -1)$ (3).
\item $I/2$: the centre of the ball (2) --- maximally mixed.
\item $\rho_{10} = \frac i2$: $r_y = 1$, i.e.\ $(0, 1, 0)$ (4), the pure state $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + i\ket1)$.
\item $\operatorname{diag}(0.75, 0.25)$: $r_z = 0.5$ (1), a mixed state on the $z$-axis.
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Q$\to$1, S$\to$2 confuses $I/2$ (centre) with a partially mixed state.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] R$\to$1, S$\to$4 gives a diagonal matrix a $y$-component, which needs an imaginary off-diagonal.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$1, S$\to$3 swaps $\ket1$ and the mixed state: $\ket1$ is pure, length 1.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Length = purity information; direction = which state.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{16}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Hermitian, unitary, projector, Kraus}
Match each matrix (List-I) with its property (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\begin{psmallmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}$ & \textbf{(1)} & unitary but not Hermitian \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $\frac12\begin{psmallmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}$ & \textbf{(2)} & Hermitian and unitary \\
\textbf{(R)} & $\begin{psmallmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & i\end{psmallmatrix}$ & \textbf{(3)} & neither Hermitian nor unitary (a Kraus operator of amplitude damping, up to a factor) \\
\textbf{(S)} & $\begin{psmallmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}$ & \textbf{(4)} & a rank-1 projector and a valid density matrix \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$1, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$3 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Hermitian, unitary, projector and density-matrix properties.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Hermitian $A = A^\dagger$; unitary $U^\dagger U = I$; projector $P^2 = P = P^\dagger$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item $X$: $X^\dagger = X$ and $X^\dagger X = I$ (2); it has trace 0, so it is not a density matrix.
\item $\ket+\!\bra+$: Hermitian, $P^2 = P$, trace 1, PSD (4); not unitary ($\det = 0$).
\item $S = \operatorname{diag}(1, i)$: $S^\dagger S = I$ but $S^\dagger = \operatorname{diag}(1, -i) \neq S$ (1).
\item $\ket0\!\bra1$: nilpotent, $\neq$ its adjoint, not invertible (3); $\sqrt\gamma\ket0\!\bra1$ is the ``jump'' of amplitude damping.
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] P$\to$4 makes $X$ a density matrix, but $\operatorname{Tr}X = 0$ and $X^2 = I \neq X$ (not a projector).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] R$\to$3 calls $S$ non-unitary, but $S^\dagger S = \operatorname{diag}(1, -i\cdot i) = I$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$1 calls $X$ non-Hermitian, but $X^\dagger = X$; and R$\to$2 calls $S$ Hermitian, but $S^\dagger = \operatorname{diag}(1, -i) \neq S$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Kraus operators need not be Hermitian or unitary; only $\sum K^\dagger K = I$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{17}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Mixed states inside the Bloch ball}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} Every mixed single-qubit state lies strictly inside the Bloch ball ($|\vec r| < 1$).\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} For $\rho = \frac12(I + \vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$ one has $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$, which equals 1 only when $|\vec r| = 1$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Purity and Bloch length.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $(\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)^2 = |\vec r|^2I$; $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true}: $\rho^2 = \frac14(I + 2\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma + (\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)^2) = \frac14((1 + |\vec r|^2)I + 2\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$ because
$(\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)^2 = |\vec r|^2I$; the trace is $\frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$. \textbf{A is true}: ``mixed'' means $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 < 1$,
which by R is exactly $|\vec r| < 1$. R is the reason for A. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] requires that R does not explain A; but A follows directly from R, since ``mixed'' means $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 < 1$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] requires R to be false, but $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$ follows from $(\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)^2 = |\vec r|^2I$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_k = 0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] requires A to be false, but no mixed state can reach the surface: $|\vec r| = 1$ forces $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = 1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Mixed $\Leftrightarrow$ inside the Bloch ball; noise shrinks Bloch vectors.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{18}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Density-matrix conditions; Born rule}
\textbf{Statement I:} Every $2\times2$ Hermitian matrix with trace 1 is a valid density matrix.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} The diagonal entries of a density matrix in the computational basis are the probabilities of the outcomes of a
computational-basis measurement.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Density-matrix conditions; Born rule for mixed states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P(k) = \operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_k\rho) = \rho_{kk}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is false}: positivity is also required; $\operatorname{diag}(1.2, -0.2)$ is Hermitian with trace 1 but has a negative eigenvalue.
\textbf{II is true}: $P(k) = \operatorname{Tr}(\ket k\!\bra k\rho) = \rho_{kk}$ (Born rule for mixed states). This is how the notebook turns an exact noisy
$\rho$ into outcome probabilities on the density-matrix path. Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] requires Statement I to be true, but I omits positivity: $\operatorname{diag}(1.2, -0.2)$ is Hermitian with trace 1 and is not a state.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] requires Statement II to be false, but $\rho_{kk} = \operatorname{Tr}(\ket k\!\bra k\rho)$ is exactly the Born-rule probability of outcome $k$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] asserts I true and II false --- exactly the reverse of the correct judgement.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Probabilities are on the diagonal; positivity is not automatic.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 19 and 20}
A qubit should have been prepared in $\ket+ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + \ket1)$. State tomography of the real (noisy)
preparation gives the density matrix
\[ \rho = \begin{pmatrix}0.55 & 0.35\\ 0.35 & 0.45\end{pmatrix}. \]
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{19}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Tomography: Bloch vector, purity}
The Bloch vector and the purity of the prepared state are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$(0.7,\ 0,\ 0.1)$ and $0.50$ & \optlabel{B}\,$(0.7,\ 0,\ 0.55)$ and $0.85$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$(0.35,\ 0,\ 0.1)$ and $0.75$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$(0.7,\ 0,\ 0.1)$ and $0.75$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $(0.7,\ 0,\ 0.1)$ and $0.75$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Bloch vector and purity of a measured density matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $r_x = 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{01}$, $r_z = \rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$; $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = \frac{1 + |\vec r|^2}{2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $r_x = 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{01} = 0.7$, $r_y = 0$ (real matrix), $r_z = 0.55 - 0.45 = 0.1$.
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2 = 0.55^2 + 0.45^2 + 2(0.35)^2 = 0.3025 + 0.2025 + 0.245 = 0.75 = \frac{1 + 0.49 + 0.01}{2}$. The vector is shorter than 1
(mixed: decoherence) and tilted towards $\ket0$ (a population imbalance, e.g.\ relaxation).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Purity $0.50$ belongs to the maximally mixed state $I/2$; here the Bloch vector has length $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.71$, so the purity is $0.75$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $r_z = 0.55$ uses $\rho_{00}$ instead of $\rho_{00} - \rho_{11}$, and $0.85$ is the fidelity with $\ket+$, not the purity.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $r_x = 0.35$ forgets the factor 2 in $r_x = 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{01}$ (and would give a different purity).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Read $\vec r$ off $\rho$, then purity from $|\vec r|$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{20}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Tomography: fidelity, probabilities}
The fidelity $\braket{+|\rho|+}$ of the preparation, and the probability that a computational-basis measurement gives $1$, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.70$ and $0.45$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.85$ and $0.45$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.92$ and $0.45$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.85$ and $0.55$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.85$ and $0.45$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fidelity with $\ket+$ and computational-basis probabilities.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\braket{+|\rho|+} = \frac{1 + r_x}{2}$; $P(1) = \rho_{11}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\braket{+|\rho|+} = \frac12(\rho_{00} + \rho_{01} + \rho_{10} + \rho_{11}) = \frac12(0.55 + 0.35 + 0.35 + 0.45) = 0.85 = \frac{1 + r_x}{2}$.
$P(1) = \rho_{11} = 0.45$. ($0.92 = \sqrt{0.85}$ is the root fidelity used in some texts; $0.70$ is $r_x$ itself.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.70$ is the Bloch component $r_x$; the fidelity is $\frac{1 + r_x}{2} = 0.85$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.92 = \sqrt{0.85}$ is the ``root fidelity'' convention; the question defines $F = \braket{+|\rho|+}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.55 = \rho_{00}$ is the probability of outcome 0; the probability of 1 is $\rho_{11} = 0.45$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $F(\ket+, \rho) = \frac{1 + r_x}{2}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\newpage

\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION B \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Quantum Noise Fundamentals \hfill Q.21--40\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{21}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Fixed points of bit flip}
Which single-qubit state is left \emph{unchanged} by the bit-flip channel $\rho \mapsto (1 - p)\rho + pX\rho X$ for every $p$?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + i\ket1)$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\ket1$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\ket0$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\ket+$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\ket+$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fixed points of a Pauli channel: eigenstates of the error operator.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Bit flip: $(r_x, r_y, r_z) \mapsto (r_x, (1-2p)r_y, (1-2p)r_z)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} A state is invariant iff $X\rho X = \rho$, i.e.\ its Bloch vector satisfies $(r_x, -r_y, -r_z) = (r_x, r_y, r_z)$: $r_y = r_z = 0$.
$\ket+$ has $\vec r = (1, 0, 0)$ (indeed $X\ket+ = \ket+$). $\ket0$, $\ket1$ have $r_z = \pm1$ and become mixed; $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + i\ket1)$ has
$r_y = 1$, which shrinks to $1 - 2p$. The eigenstates of the error operator are immune to that error.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] This state has $r_y = 1$, which shrinks to $1 - 2p$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\ket1$ has $r_z = -1$, which shrinks as well.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $\ket0$ has $r_z = 1$, which shrinks to $1 - 2p$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} States along the error's axis are immune to it.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{22}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Phase flip on $\ket+$}
A phase-flip channel with $p = 0.1$ acts on $\ket+$. The state is then measured in the $X$ basis. The probability of the
outcome ``$+$'' is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.95$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.0$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.8$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.9$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.9$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Phase flips act like $\ket+ \leftrightarrow \ket-$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho' = (1-p)\rho + pZ\rho Z$; $\langle X\rangle \mapsto (1-2p)\langle X\rangle$; $P(+) = \frac{1 + \langle X\rangle}{2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\rho' = 0.9\ket+\!\bra+ + 0.1Z\ket+\!\bra+Z = 0.9\ket+\!\bra+ + 0.1\ket-\!\bra-$ (since $Z\ket+ = \ket-$). So $P(+) = 0.9$ and
$\langle X\rangle = 0.9 - 0.1 = 1 - 2p = 0.8$. In the $Z$ basis nothing changes ($P(0) = P(1) = \frac12$): phase errors are invisible there.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.95$ uses $p/2$ as the error probability; a $Z$ applied with probability $p$ turns $\ket+$ into $\ket-$ with probability $p$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.0$ would mean the phase flip had no effect; that is true only for $Z$-basis measurements, not in the $X$ basis.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.8 = 1 - 2p$ is the expectation value $\langle X\rangle = P(+) - P(-)$, not the probability $P(+)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Phase errors appear only in a rotated basis.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{23}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Depolarizing flip probability}
A depolarizing channel $\rho \mapsto (1 - p)\rho + \frac p3(X\rho X + Y\rho Y + Z\rho Z)$ with $p = 0.03$ acts on $\ket0$. The probability of
then measuring $1$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.03$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.04$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.02$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.01$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.02$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Depolarizing channel in CUDA-Q's convention.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathcal E(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + \frac p3(X\rho X + Y\rho Y + Z\rho Z)$, $\vec r \mapsto (1 - \frac{4p}{3})\vec r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $X$ and $Y$ flip $\ket0$ to $\ket1$ (up to a phase), $Z$ does not. So $P(1) = \frac p3 + \frac p3 = \frac{2p}{3} = 0.02$.
Equivalently the Bloch vector shrinks by $1 - \frac{4p}{3} = 0.96$: $r_z = 0.96$, $P(1) = \frac{1 - r_z}{2} = 0.02$.
(This is CUDA-Q's \texttt{DepolarizationChannel(p)} convention; the same channel is $\rho \mapsto (1 - \lambda)\rho + \lambda\frac I2$ with $\lambda = \frac{4p}{3}$.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.03 = p$ treats all three Paulis as flips, but $Z\ket0 = \ket0$ does not change the outcome.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.04 = \frac{4p}{3}$ is the reduction $1 - r_z$ of the Bloch component, twice the flip probability $\frac{1 - r_z}{2}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.01 = p/3$ counts only $X$; $Y = iXZ$ also maps $\ket0$ to $\ket1$ (up to a phase).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Two of the three Paulis flip a $Z$ outcome: $P = \frac{2p}{3}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{24}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Amplitude damping on $\ket+$}
Amplitude damping with $\gamma = 0.36$ acts on $\ket+$. The resulting density matrix is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.68 & 0.40\\ 0.40 & 0.32\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.68 & 0.32\\ 0.32 & 0.32\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.50 & 0.40\\ 0.40 & 0.50\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.68 & 0.50\\ 0.50 & 0.32\end{pmatrix}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $\begin{pmatrix}0.68 & 0.40\\ 0.40 & 0.32\end{pmatrix}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Amplitude damping: energy relaxation to $\ket0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho_{11} \mapsto (1-\gamma)\rho_{11}$, $\rho_{00} \mapsto \rho_{00} + \gamma\rho_{11}$, $\rho_{01} \mapsto \sqrt{1-\gamma}\rho_{01}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} With $K_0 = \operatorname{diag}(1, \sqrt{1-\gamma})$, $K_1 = \sqrt\gamma\ket0\!\bra1$:
$\rho_{11}' = (1 - \gamma)\rho_{11}$, $\rho_{00}' = \rho_{00} + \gamma\rho_{11}$, $\rho_{01}' = \sqrt{1 - \gamma}\,\rho_{01}$.
For $\ket+$ ($\rho_{ij} = \frac12$): $\rho_{11}' = 0.64\cdot0.5 = 0.32$, $\rho_{00}' = 0.5 + 0.18 = 0.68$, $\rho_{01}' = 0.8\cdot0.5 = 0.40$.
Populations move towards $\ket0$ and the coherence shrinks by $\sqrt{1 - \gamma}$, not by $1 - \gamma$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Scaling the coherence by $1 - \gamma = 0.64$ instead of $\sqrt{1-\gamma} = 0.8$ confuses the population decay with the amplitude decay.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Leaving the populations at $0.5$ ignores the jump $\ket1 \to \ket0$; that would be phase damping, not amplitude damping.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Keeping the coherence at $0.5$ ignores that the no-jump operator $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sqrt{1-\gamma})$ also shrinks $\rho_{01}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $T_1$ decay also costs coherence, at half the rate.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{25}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Phase damping $\equiv$ phase flip}
Phase damping with parameter $\lambda$ multiplies the off-diagonal elements by $\sqrt{1 - \lambda}$; a phase-flip channel multiplies them by $1 - 2p$.
The phase-flip probability $p$ that has the same effect as phase damping with $\lambda = 0.36$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.18$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.36$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.10$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.20$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.10$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Different Kraus sets can represent the same channel.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Phase flip: coherence $\times(1-2p)$; phase damping: coherence $\times\sqrt{1-\lambda}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Both channels leave the populations unchanged, so they are equal iff they scale the coherence by the same factor:
$1 - 2p = \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 0.8 \Rightarrow p = 0.1$. Phase damping and the phase-flip channel are the same channel in different Kraus
representations (Kraus operators are not unique).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.18 = \lambda/2$ equates $2p$ with $\lambda$, which is only the first-order approximation of $1 - 2p = \sqrt{1-\lambda}$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.36$ sets $p = \lambda$; then $1 - 2p = 0.28 \neq 0.8$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.20 = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \lambda}$ forgets the factor 2 in the phase-flip coherence factor $1 - 2p$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Phase damping $\equiv$ phase flip with $1 - 2p = \sqrt{1-\lambda}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{26}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$T_1$ half-life}
A qubit with $T_1 = 50\,\mu$s starts in $\ket1$. After what time is $P(1) = \frac12$?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$50\,\mu$s & \optlabel{B}\,$69.3\,\mu$s & \optlabel{C}\,$25\,\mu$s & \correctlabel{D}\,$34.7\,\mu$s
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $34.7\,\mu$s

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Exponential $T_1$ decay and half-life.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P_1(t) = e^{-t/T_1}$; $t_{1/2} = T_1\ln2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $P(1) = e^{-t/T_1} = \frac12 \Rightarrow t = T_1\ln2 = 50\times0.693 = 34.7\,\mu$s. At $t = T_1$ the population is $e^{-1} = 0.368$, not $\frac12$;
$69.3\,\mu$s would give $\frac14$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $50\,\mu$s $= T_1$ gives $P(1) = e^{-1} = 0.368$, not $\frac12$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $69.3\,\mu$s $= 2T_1\ln2$ is two half-lives: $P(1) = \frac14$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $25\,\mu$s $= T_1/2$ assumes linear decay; exponential decay gives $e^{-0.5} = 0.61$ at that time.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Half-life $= 0.693\,T_1$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{27}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$T_2$ from $T_1$ and $T_\varphi$}
A qubit has $T_1 = 100\,\mu$s and pure-dephasing time $T_\varphi = 200\,\mu$s. Using $\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\varphi}$, $T_2$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$150\,\mu$s & \optlabel{B}\,$66.7\,\mu$s & \optlabel{C}\,$200\,\mu$s & \correctlabel{D}\,$100\,\mu$s
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $100\,\mu$s

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Relationship between $T_1$, $T_2$ and pure dephasing.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\varphi}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{200} + \frac{1}{200} = \frac{1}{100}\ \mu\text{s}^{-1}$, so $T_2 = 100\,\mu$s. Relaxation contributes only $\frac{1}{2T_1}$ because amplitude
damping multiplies the coherence by $\sqrt{1 - \gamma} \approx e^{-t/2T_1}$. Using $\frac1{T_1}$ instead would give $66.7\,\mu$s.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $150\,\mu$s averages the two times; decoherence \emph{rates} add, times do not.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $66.7\,\mu$s uses $\frac{1}{T_1}$ instead of $\frac{1}{2T_1}$ for the relaxation contribution to dephasing.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $200\,\mu$s $= T_\varphi$ ignores the dephasing caused by relaxation itself.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Add rates, not times; relaxation contributes half its rate to dephasing.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{28}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Constraint $T_2 \le 2T_1$}
Which pair $(T_1, T_2)$ is \emph{physically impossible} in the standard model?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$T_1 = 100\,\mu$s, $T_2 = 30\,\mu$s & \correctlabel{B}\,$T_1 = 50\,\mu$s, $T_2 = 120\,\mu$s \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$T_1 = 50\,\mu$s, $T_2 = 100\,\mu$s & \optlabel{D}\,$T_1 = 80\,\mu$s, $T_2 = 80\,\mu$s
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $T_1 = 50\,\mu$s, $T_2 = 120\,\mu$s

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Physical constraint $T_2 \le 2T_1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\frac{1}{T_\varphi} = \frac1{T_2} - \frac{1}{2T_1} \ge 0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Since $\frac1{T_\varphi} = \frac1{T_2} - \frac1{2T_1} \ge 0$, every qubit satisfies $T_2 \le 2T_1$. $120 > 2\times50 = 100$ violates it. $T_2 = 2T_1$
(no pure dephasing) is the allowed limit; $T_2 < T_1$ is common in practice.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $T_2 = 30\,\mu$s $< T_1 = 100\,\mu$s is common in real devices: strong pure dephasing.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $T_2 = 2T_1 = 100\,\mu$s is the allowed limit of a qubit without pure dephasing ($T_\varphi = \infty$).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $T_2 = T_1$ satisfies $T_2 \le 2T_1$ with $\frac1{T_\varphi} = \frac{1}{2T_1} > 0$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $T_2$ can never exceed $2T_1$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{29}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Coherence-limited depth}
Gates take $50$ ns and the qubit has $T_2 = 100\,\mu$s. Requiring the coherence factor $e^{-t/T_2}$ to stay at least $0.9$, the largest number of
sequential gates is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$210$ & \optlabel{B}\,$21$ & \optlabel{C}\,$2000$ & \optlabel{D}\,$105$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $210$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Coherence-limited circuit depth.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $e^{-nt_g/T_2} \ge F \Rightarrow n \le \frac{T_2\ln(1/F)}{t_g}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $e^{-nt_g/T_2} \ge 0.9 \Leftrightarrow n \le \frac{T_2\ln(1/0.9)}{t_g} = \frac{100\,\mu\text{s}\times0.1054}{0.05\,\mu\text{s}} = 210.7$, so about $210$ gates.
$T_2/t_g = 2000$ is the number of gates in one $T_2$, when the coherence has already fallen to $e^{-1} = 0.37$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $21$ is ten times too small: it corresponds to a target coherence of about $0.99$ ($\ln(1/0.99) = 0.01$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2000 = T_2/t_g$ is the number of gates in one $T_2$; by then the coherence has decayed to $e^{-1} = 0.37$, far below $0.9$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $105$ uses $\frac12\ln(1/0.9)$, i.e.\ treats the coherence as decaying twice as fast as $e^{-t/T_2}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Depth budget $\approx (T_2/t_g)\ln(1/F)$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{30}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Readout error probabilities}
A detector reads $1$ when the qubit is in $\ket0$ with probability $0.02$, and reads $0$ when it is in $\ket1$ with probability $0.05$. For a perfectly
prepared $\ket+$, the probability of reading $1$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.515$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.475$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.485$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.500$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.485$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Classical readout error as a confusion matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P(\text{read }1) = \sum_sP(s)P(1|s)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Law of total probability: $P(\text{read }1) = P(0)P(1|0) + P(1)P(1|1) = 0.5(0.02) + 0.5(0.95) = 0.01 + 0.475 = 0.485$.
Readout errors are classical (they act on the recorded bit) and are usually \emph{asymmetric}: $\ket1$ can relax during the measurement.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.515 = 0.5(0.05) + 0.5(0.98)$ swaps the roles of the two error rates.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.475 = 0.5\times0.95$ forgets the contribution $0.5\times0.02$ of $\ket0$ shots misread as 1.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.5$ assumes a perfect detector; the two error rates are unequal, so they do not cancel.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Readout errors mix outcome probabilities through a stochastic matrix.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{31}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Readout errors on GHZ}
A perfect 3-qubit GHZ state is measured with the readout errors of the previous question ($P(1|0) = 0.02$, $P(0|1) = 0.05$, independent per qubit).
The probability of observing $000$ or $111$ is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.899$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.950$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.857$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.941$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.899$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Readout errors on several qubits multiply.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P(\text{all correct}) = \prod_i(1 - e_i)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $P(000\text{ read correctly}) = 0.98^3 = 0.9412$, $P(111\text{ read correctly}) = 0.95^3 = 0.8574$. With probability $\frac12$ each:
$\frac12(0.9412 + 0.8574) = 0.8993$; the cross terms ($000 \to 111$: $0.02^3$, $111 \to 000$: $0.05^3$) add only $7\times10^{-5}$. Readout
errors grow with the number of measured qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.95$ is the single-qubit probability of reading $\ket1$ correctly; three qubits must all be read correctly.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.857 = 0.95^3$ is the probability for the $111$ branch only.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.941 = 0.98^3$ is the probability for the $000$ branch only, but GHZ gives $111$ half of the time.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Readout fidelity decays exponentially with qubit number.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{32}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Coherent vs incoherent errors}
Which of the following is a \emph{coherent} (unitary) error rather than decoherence or a measurement error?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] the discriminator labelling a $\ket1$ outcome as $0$
\item[\correctlabel{B}] a systematic over-rotation of every $X$ gate caused by a miscalibrated pulse amplitude
\item[\optlabel{C}] a random phase that differs from shot to shot and averages to dephasing
\item[\optlabel{D}] energy relaxation of $\ket1$ to $\ket0$ (a $T_1$ process)
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} a systematic over-rotation of every $X$ gate caused by a miscalibrated pulse amplitude

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Coherent vs incoherent errors vs readout errors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Coherent: $\rho \mapsto U_\varepsilon\rho U_\varepsilon^\dagger$; stochastic: $\sum_kp_kP_k\rho P_k$; readout: confusion matrix on outcomes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} A coherent error is a deterministic, unitary deviation $U_{\text{actual}} = U\,e^{-i\varepsilon H}$, identical in every run; it keeps the state pure
and its effects can add up in \emph{amplitude} (quadratically in probability). $T_1$ relaxation is non-unitary decoherence; a phase that is random from run
to run produces a mixed state (stochastic dephasing); a misassigned outcome is a classical readout error.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Misassignment happens after the quantum measurement.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] A phase random from shot to shot is stochastic dephasing.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $T_1$ relaxation is non-unitary (amplitude damping).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Systematic and the same every time $\Rightarrow$ coherent.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{33}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Two-qubit depolarizing marginal}
After a CNOT, CUDA-Q's \texttt{Depolarization2(p)} applies each of the 15 non-identity two-qubit Paulis with probability $p/15$. For $p = 0.015$, the
probability that the outcome of a $Z$-basis measurement of the control qubit is flipped by this error is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.010$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.008$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.0075$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.015$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.008$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Two-qubit depolarizing channel and its marginal effect.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathcal E_2(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + \frac{p}{15}\sum_{P\neq II}P\rho P$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The $Z$ outcome of the control flips iff the Pauli on the control is $X$ or $Y$. Of the 15 non-identity pairs $P_c\otimes P_t$, those with
$P_c \in \{X, Y\}$ are $2\times4 = 8$. Probability $= 8\cdot\frac{p}{15} = \frac{8(0.015)}{15} = 0.008$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.010 = \frac{2p}{3}$ is the flip probability of the \emph{single-qubit} depolarizing channel, not the marginal of the two-qubit one ($\frac{8}{15}p$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.0075 = \frac p2$ assumes half of the Paulis flip the control; the correct fraction is $\frac{8}{15}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.015 = p$ counts all 15 Paulis as flipping the control, but $IX, IY, IZ, ZI, \dots$ ($7$ of them) leave its $Z$ outcome unchanged.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Count the Paulis that anticommute with the measured observable.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{34}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Phase errors and the $X$ basis}
A 15-qubit GHZ state suffers only phase-flip noise. Which measurement reveals the errors?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] the parity $\langle X^{\otimes15}\rangle$ measured after a Hadamard on every qubit
\item[\optlabel{B}] the probability $P(0\cdots0)$ alone
\item[\optlabel{C}] the number of distinct outcomes in the $Z$ basis
\item[\optlabel{D}] the $Z$-basis population $P(0\cdots0) + P(1\cdots1)$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} the parity $\langle X^{\otimes15}\rangle$ measured after a Hadamard on every qubit

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Which errors each measurement basis can see.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $[Z, Z_i] = 0$; $Z_i(\ket{0\cdots0} + \ket{1\cdots1}) = \ket{0\cdots0} - \ket{1\cdots1}$; $\langle X^{\otimes N}\rangle \to -\langle X^{\otimes N}\rangle$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $Z$ errors commute with $Z$-basis measurements, so all $Z$-basis statistics are unchanged: the population stays 1 and only the outcomes $0\cdots0$,
$1\cdots1$ occur. A single $Z$ error turns $\ket{0\cdots0} + \ket{1\cdots1}$ into $\ket{0\cdots0} - \ket{1\cdots1}$, which flips the sign of $\langle X^{\otimes N}\rangle$.
This is why \texttt{Noise\_Simulation.ipynb} also measures in the $X$ basis (\texttt{MEASURE\_X\_BASIS = True}).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $P(0\cdots0)$ stays $\frac12$; $\ket{0\cdots0} \pm \ket{1\cdots1}$ have identical $Z$ statistics.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The number of distinct $Z$-basis outcomes stays 2 ($0\cdots0$ and $1\cdots1$), whatever the phase errors.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The $Z$-basis population stays exactly 1: $Z$ errors only change phases.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Measure in a second basis to see phase errors.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{35}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Kraus operators of channels}
Match each channel (List-I) with a set of Kraus operators (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & bit flip & \textbf{(1)} & $\operatorname{diag}(1, \sqrt{1-\lambda})$, $\operatorname{diag}(0, \sqrt\lambda)$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & phase flip & \textbf{(2)} & $\sqrt{1-p}\,I$, $\sqrt p\,Z$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & amplitude damping & \textbf{(3)} & $\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\end{psmallmatrix}$, $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&\sqrt\gamma\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & phase damping & \textbf{(4)} & $\sqrt{1-p}\,I$, $\sqrt p\,X$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$1, R$\to$3, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$3, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Kraus representations of the standard channels.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Completeness $\sum K^\dagger K = I$ for each set.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item bit flip: apply $X$ with probability $p$ (4);
\item phase flip: apply $Z$ with probability $p$ (2);
\item amplitude damping: the ``jump'' $\sqrt\gamma\ket0\!\bra1$ and the no-jump $K_0$ (3);
\item phase damping: diagonal Kraus operators, populations untouched, coherence $\times\sqrt{1-\lambda}$ (1).
\end{itemize}
Each set satisfies $\sum K^\dagger K = I$. Hence P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$3, S$\to$1.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Q$\to$1, S$\to$2 gives the phase flip the diagonal damping operators and vice versa; the channels are equivalent but the question asks for the stated Kraus forms.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$2, Q$\to$4 swaps $X$ and $Z$: the bit flip applies $X$, the phase flip applies $Z$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] R$\to$1, S$\to$3 swaps amplitude and phase damping; only amplitude damping has the off-diagonal jump $\ket0\!\bra1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Bit flip $X$, phase flip $Z$, AD jump $\ket0\!\bra1$, PD diagonal.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{36}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Channels on the Bloch ball}
Match each channel (List-I) with its action on the Bloch vector $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & depolarizing (CUDA-Q convention, $p$) & \textbf{(1)} & $r_x, r_y$ scaled, $r_z$ unchanged \\
\textbf{(Q)} & amplitude damping ($\gamma$) & \textbf{(2)} & all three components multiplied by the same factor $1 - \frac{4p}{3}$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & phase damping ($\lambda$) & \textbf{(3)} & $r_x$ unchanged, $r_y$ and $r_z$ multiplied by $1 - 2p$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & bit flip ($p$) & \textbf{(4)} & $r_x, r_y$ multiplied by $\sqrt{1-\gamma}$, $r_z \mapsto \gamma + (1-\gamma)r_z$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Geometric action of channels on the Bloch ball.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Depolarizing $\vec r \mapsto (1 - \frac{4p}{3})\vec r$; AD $r_z \mapsto \gamma + (1-\gamma)r_z$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item depolarizing: an isotropic shrink of the whole ball (2);
\item amplitude damping: shrinks and pushes the ball towards the north pole $\ket0$ --- the only non-unital one here (4);
\item phase damping: shrinks towards the $z$-axis (1);
\item bit flip: shrinks towards the $x$-axis (3).
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps AD and PD: only AD shifts the centre.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] R$\to$3, S$\to$1: PD keeps $r_z$, bit flip keeps $r_x$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$3, S$\to$2 gives depolarizing an axis; it is isotropic.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Only amplitude damping moves the centre of the ball.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{37}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Non-unital amplitude damping}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} Amplitude damping is not unital: it does not map the maximally mixed state $I/2$ to itself.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} Amplitude damping multiplies the off-diagonal elements of $\rho$ by $\sqrt{1 - \gamma}$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Unital vs non-unital channels.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Unital: $\mathcal E(I) = I$; AD: $\mathcal E(I/2) = \operatorname{diag}(\frac{1+\gamma}2, \frac{1-\gamma}2)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true}: $I/2 \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(\frac{1+\gamma}{2}, \frac{1-\gamma}{2}) \neq I/2$ --- energy flows to $\ket0$.
\textbf{R is true} as well, but it does not explain A: phase damping shrinks the off-diagonals in the same way and \emph{is} unital. Non-unitality
comes from the population transfer $\rho_{00} \mapsto \rho_{00} + \gamma\rho_{11}$ (the jump operator $\ket0\!\bra1$). Answer: (B).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs R to explain A; phase damping shows that coherence decay does not imply non-unitality.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs R false; the $\sqrt{1-\gamma}$ factor is correct.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs A false; AD is the standard non-unital channel.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Non-unital = drives towards a preferred state (here $\ket0$).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{38}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Complete dephasing vs unitary $Z$}
\textbf{Statement I:} The phase-flip channel with $p = \frac12$ maps every single-qubit state to a state with zero off-diagonal elements.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} The phase-flip channel with $p = 1$ destroys all quantum information.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Statement I is true, but Statement II is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Unitary vs random errors; complete dephasing.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Coherence $\times(1 - 2p)$; $p = 1$: $\rho \mapsto Z\rho Z$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true}: the coherence is multiplied by $1 - 2p = 0$ (complete dephasing). \textbf{II is false}: with $p = 1$ the channel is
$\rho \mapsto Z\rho Z$, a \emph{unitary} that can be undone by applying $Z$ again. Information is lost only when the error is random ($0 < p < 1$),
most for $p = \frac12$. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] requires II to be true, but $\rho \mapsto Z\rho Z$ is reversible by applying $Z$ again.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] requires I to be false, but at $p = \frac12$ the coherence factor $1 - 2p$ is exactly 0.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] asserts I false and II true --- exactly the reverse of the correct judgement.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Information loss needs randomness, maximal at $p = \frac12$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 39 and 40}
A superconducting qubit has $T_1 = 80\,\mu$s and $T_2 = 60\,\mu$s. It is prepared in $\ket+$ and then idles for $t = 20\,\mu$s.
Use the standard model: populations relax towards $\ket0$ as $\rho_{11}(t) = \rho_{11}(0)e^{-t/T_1}$, and the coherence decays as
$|\rho_{01}(t)| = |\rho_{01}(0)|e^{-t/T_2}$, with $\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\varphi}$ ($T_\varphi$ = pure-dephasing time).
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{39}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{$T_1$/$T_2$ decay of $\ket+$}
After the idle period, $\rho_{11}$ and $|\rho_{01}|$ are approximately
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.389$ and $0.358$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.500$ and $0.358$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.389$ and $0.316$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.389$ and $0.389$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.389$ and $0.358$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Applying $T_1$ and $T_2$ decay to a state.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\rho_{11}(t) = \rho_{11}(0)e^{-t/T_1}$, $|\rho_{01}(t)| = |\rho_{01}(0)|e^{-t/T_2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\rho_{11}(0) = |\rho_{01}(0)| = \frac12$ for $\ket+$. $\rho_{11} = \frac12e^{-20/80} = \frac12e^{-0.25} = 0.389$.
$|\rho_{01}| = \frac12e^{-20/60} = \frac12e^{-1/3} = 0.358$. The $T_2$ decay already \emph{includes} the relaxation contribution; multiplying by
$e^{-t/2T_1}$ again would double-count it ($0.316$).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\rho_{11} = 0.5$ assumes no relaxation; with $T_1 = 80\,\mu$s, $e^{-20/80} = 0.78$ of the excited population survives.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.316$ multiplies the $T_2$ decay by an extra $e^{-t/2T_1}$; $T_2$ already contains the relaxation contribution.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.389$ for the coherence uses $e^{-t/T_1}$; coherence decays with $T_2$, not $T_1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $T_1$ for populations, $T_2$ for coherences.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{40}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Fidelity and $T_\varphi$}
The fidelity $\braket{+|\rho|+}$ after the idle period, and the pure-dephasing time $T_\varphi$, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.889$ and $96\,\mu$s & \optlabel{B}\,$0.716$ and $96\,\mu$s \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$0.858$ and $96\,\mu$s & \optlabel{D}\,$0.858$ and $43.6\,\mu$s
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.858$ and $96\,\mu$s

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fidelity with $\ket+$; extracting $T_\varphi$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $F = \frac12 + \operatorname{Re}\rho_{01}$; $\frac1{T_\varphi} = \frac1{T_2} - \frac1{2T_1}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\braket{+|\rho|+} = \frac12(\rho_{00} + \rho_{11}) + \operatorname{Re}\rho_{01} = \frac12 + 0.358 = 0.858$ (populations sum to 1 whatever their split).
$\frac{1}{T_\varphi} = \frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{2T_1} = \frac{1}{60} - \frac{1}{160} = 0.01667 - 0.00625 = 0.01042\ \mu\text{s}^{-1}$, so $T_\varphi = 96\,\mu$s.
Adding instead of subtracting gives $43.6\,\mu$s.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.889 = \frac12 + \rho_{11}$ uses a population instead of the coherence $\operatorname{Re}\rho_{01}$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.716 = 2|\rho_{01}|$ forgets the constant $\frac12$ from $\frac12(\rho_{00} + \rho_{11})$ and halving the coherence term.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $43.6\,\mu$s adds the rates $\frac1{T_2} + \frac{1}{2T_1}$ instead of subtracting them.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Fidelity with $\ket+$ depends only on the coherence.
\end{solbox}
\qsep
