\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION C \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Noise Models and Simulation \hfill Q.41--60\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{41}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{CUDA-Q depolarizing convention}
On the target \texttt{density-matrix-cpu} a kernel prepares $\ket0$ and applies \texttt{rx(t, q[0])}, with \texttt{t = 0.0} passed as a kernel
argument. The noise model attaches \texttt{cudaq.DepolarizationChannel(0.3)} to every \texttt{rx}. \texttt{cudaq.observe} of $Z$ returns
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.7$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.6$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$1.0$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.6$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} CUDA-Q's depolarizing convention; channels act after the gate.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\vec r \mapsto (1 - \frac{4p}{3})\vec r$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \texttt{rx(0)} is the identity, so the state before the channel is $\ket0$ ($r_z = 1$). CUDA-Q's depolarizing channel has Kraus operators
$\sqrt{1-p}\,I$, $\sqrt{p/3}\,X$, $\sqrt{p/3}\,Y$, $\sqrt{p/3}\,Z$; it multiplies the Bloch vector by $1 - \frac{4p}{3} = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$.
So $\langle Z\rangle = 0.6$ (measured with CUDA-Q 0.16 for the lecture). $\rho_{11} = \frac{2p}{3} = 0.2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.7 = 1 - p$ is the weight of the identity Kraus operator, not $\langle Z\rangle$; the $X$ and $Y$ branches flip $Z$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.4 = 1 - 2p$ is the factor of a bit-flip (or phase-flip) channel with probability $p$, not of the depolarizing channel.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $1.0$ would mean the noise never acted --- which is what happens when the identity gate is removed by the compiler (Question Q.42).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $\langle Z\rangle = 1 - \frac{4p}{3}$ on $\ket0$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{42}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Constant identity gates and noise}
The same experiment is repeated, but the kernel now contains \texttt{rx(0.0, q[0])} with the angle written as a \emph{literal constant}. With CUDA-Q 0.16
the result is $\langle Z\rangle = 1.0$. The best explanation is
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] the compiler removes the constant identity rotation, so there is no \texttt{rx} gate left to carry the noise channel
\item[\optlabel{B}] noise channels are applied only before a gate, never after it
\item[\optlabel{C}] \texttt{density-matrix-cpu} ignores noise models
\item[\optlabel{D}] the depolarizing channel acts only on non-zero rotation angles by definition
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} the compiler removes the constant identity rotation, so there is no \texttt{rx} gate left to carry the noise channel

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Noise channels attach to gates of the compiled circuit.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Channel fires $\Leftrightarrow$ the gate survives compilation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Noise models attach channels to \emph{gate occurrences} in the compiled circuit. A rotation by a constant $0$ is an identity and is optimised away
during compilation, so the channel never fires; with a run-time argument the gate survives (Question Q.41). The channel itself does not depend on the
angle, the density-matrix target does apply noise, and channels are applied \emph{after} the gate. The lecture's experiments therefore pass idle angles
as arguments.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] CUDA-Q applies the channel after each matching gate.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The same target applies noise when the angle is an argument.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The channel's Kraus operators do not depend on the angle.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Pass identity angles as arguments, or the idle gate (and its noise) disappears.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{43}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{CPTP check}
Which set of operators defines a valid (completely positive, trace-preserving) quantum channel?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $\Big\{\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&0.6\end{psmallmatrix},\ \begin{psmallmatrix}0&0.6\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}\Big\}$
\item[\optlabel{B}] $\{I,\ \sqrt{0.1}\,X\}$
\item[\optlabel{C}] $\{\sqrt{0.5}\,I,\ \sqrt{0.5}\,X,\ \sqrt{0.5}\,Z\}$
\item[\correctlabel{D}] $\{\sqrt{0.7}\,I,\ \sqrt{0.3}\,Y\}$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\{\sqrt{0.7}\,I,\ \sqrt{0.3}\,Y\}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} CPTP condition.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\sum_kK_k^\dagger K_k = I$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Any map $\rho \mapsto \sum K\rho K^\dagger$ is completely positive; it is trace preserving iff $\sum K^\dagger K = I$.
$0.7I + 0.3Y^2 = I$ \checkmark. $I + 0.1X^2 = 1.1I$; $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0.36) + \operatorname{diag}(0, 0.36) = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.72)$; $0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5$:
the other three create or destroy probability. The first is the bit-phase-flip channel with $p = 0.3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Here $\sum K^\dagger K = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.36 + 0.36) = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0.72)$: probability is lost from $\ket1$ (it would need $0.8$ in the jump operator).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\{I, \sqrt{0.1}X\}$: $\sum K^\dagger K = I + 0.1I = 1.1I$, so the trace grows by 10\,\%.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5$: $\sum K^\dagger K = 1.5I$ creates probability.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Check $\sum K^\dagger K = I$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{44}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Applying the bit-flip channel}
The bit-flip channel with $p = 0.2$ acts on $\rho = \begin{pmatrix}0.9 & 0.3\\ 0.3 & 0.1\end{pmatrix}$. The output is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.74 & 0.18\\ 0.18 & 0.26\end{pmatrix}$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.74 & 0.30\\ 0.30 & 0.26\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.82 & 0.30\\ 0.30 & 0.18\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0.90 & 0.18\\ 0.18 & 0.10\end{pmatrix}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\begin{pmatrix}0.74 & 0.30\\ 0.30 & 0.26\end{pmatrix}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Applying a Kraus channel to a matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathcal E(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + pX\rho X$; $X\rho X$ swaps rows and columns.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $X\rho X$ swaps both rows and columns: $\begin{psmallmatrix}0.1&0.3\\0.3&0.9\end{psmallmatrix}$. Then
$0.8\rho + 0.2X\rho X = \begin{psmallmatrix}0.72 + 0.02 & 0.24 + 0.06\\ 0.24 + 0.06 & 0.08 + 0.18\end{psmallmatrix} = \begin{psmallmatrix}0.74 & 0.30\\ 0.30 & 0.26\end{psmallmatrix}$.
The real off-diagonal ($r_x = 0.6$) is untouched; $r_z$ shrinks from $0.8$ to $0.8(1 - 2p) = 0.48$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Multiplying the off-diagonal by $0.6$ is what a phase flip (or $r_x$ shrink) would do; a bit flip keeps $r_x$ and the real off-diagonal.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] This corresponds to $p = 0.1$: $0.9\rho + 0.1X\rho X = \begin{psmallmatrix}0.82&0.3\\0.3&0.18\end{psmallmatrix}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] This is the phase-flip result: populations unchanged and coherence $\times(1 - 2p)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Bit flips mix the populations, keep $r_x$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{45}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Composing depolarizing channels}
Two depolarizing channels (CUDA-Q convention) with $p_1 = 0.03$ and $p_2 = 0.06$ act one after the other. They equal a single depolarizing channel with $p$ equal to
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.1168$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.0882$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.0876$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.0900$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.0876$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Composition of depolarizing channels.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Shrink factors multiply: $(1 - \frac{4p_1}{3})(1 - \frac{4p_2}{3})$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each channel multiplies the Bloch vector by $1 - \frac{4p}{3}$: $0.96$ and $0.92$. Composed: $0.96\times0.92 = 0.8832 = 1 - \frac{4p}{3}$, so
$p = \frac34(1 - 0.8832) = 0.0876$. Probabilities do not simply add ($0.09$); composing ``no-error'' probabilities, $1 - 0.97\cdot0.94 = 0.0882$, ignores that two
Pauli errors can cancel.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.1168 = 1 - 0.8832$ is the reduction of the Bloch length, i.e.\ $\frac{4p}{3}$, not $p$ itself.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.0882 = 1 - 0.97\times0.94$ composes the \emph{no-error} probabilities and ignores that, e.g., $X$ followed by $X$ gives no error.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.09 = p_1 + p_2$: error probabilities do not simply add, because two errors can combine into the identity or another Pauli.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Compose channels by multiplying their Bloch shrink factors.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{46}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Notebook: depolarizing $(1-p)^G$}
In \texttt{Noise\_Simulation.ipynb} the 15-qubit GHZ circuit has $G$ noisy gate locations (1 Hadamard and 14 CNOTs, each followed by a depolarizing channel).
The notebook's no-error probability $(1 - p)^G$ at $p = 0.02$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.7000$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.9800$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.7386$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.5455$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.7386$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Error-free probability for the notebook's depolarizing GHZ.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $(1-p)^{g_1}(1-p)^{g_2}$ with $g_1 = 1$, $g_2 = 14$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For depolarizing noise each gate location (one- or two-qubit) fails with probability $p$, so $G = 1 + 14 = 15$ and
$(0.98)^{15} = e^{15\ln0.98} = e^{-0.3030} = 0.7386$ (printed in the notebook). $1 - 15p = 0.70$ is the linear approximation; $0.98^{30} = 0.5455$
would count two failure chances per CNOT, which is the rule the notebook uses for bit-flip and phase-flip noise, not for depolarizing noise.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.70 = 1 - Gp$ is the first-order approximation $(1-p)^G \approx 1 - Gp$, inaccurate at $Gp = 0.3$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.98$ counts a single gate location instead of $G = 15$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.5455 = 0.98^{30}$ gives each CNOT two failure chances; for depolarizing noise the notebook uses one joint channel per CNOT.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Depolarizing: one failure chance per gate location.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{47}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Notebook: bit-flip $(1-p)^{29}$}
For \texttt{NOISE\_MODEL = "bit\_flip"}, the notebook's CNOT channel is \texttt{Pauli2} with probabilities $p(1-p)$ for $IX$ and $XI$ and $p^2$ for $XX$. The
no-error probability of the 15-qubit GHZ circuit at $p = 0.01$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.7472$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.8601$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.7397$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.9801$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.7472$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Two-qubit bit-flip channel as independent flips.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $p(1-p) + p(1-p) + p^2 = 1 - (1-p)^2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The CNOT channel equals independent bit flips on both qubits: no error with probability $(1-p)^2$. With one Hadamard and 14 CNOTs:
$(1-p)\cdot(1-p)^{2\cdot14} = (1-p)^{29} = 0.99^{29} = e^{-0.2915} = 0.7472$. This is the notebook's \texttt{no\_error\_probability} for non-depolarizing
kinds ($1 - (1-p)^2$ per two-qubit gate). $0.8601$ is the depolarizing value.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.8601 = 0.99^{15}$ is the depolarizing result (one failure chance per CNOT).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.99^{30}$ counts the Hadamard as a two-qubit location; it has one failure chance, giving $1 + 2\times14 = 29$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.9801 = 0.99^2$ counts only one CNOT (two independent flips) and ignores the other 13 CNOTs and the Hadamard.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Independent flips on both CNOT qubits: $(1-p)^{29}$ in total.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{48}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Density-matrix memory}
The density-matrix method stores $4^N$ complex numbers of 16 bytes. The memory for $N = 13$ qubits is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$1.07$ GB & \optlabel{B}\,$131$ kB & \optlabel{C}\,$268$ MB & \optlabel{D}\,$4.29$ GB
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $1.07$ GB

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Density-matrix memory.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $16\cdot4^N$ bytes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $16\times4^{13} = 16\times67\,108\,864 = 1.074\times10^9$ bytes $\approx 1.07$ GB. $131$ kB is a state vector ($16\cdot2^{13}$); $268$ MB is $N = 12$ and
$4.29$ GB is $N = 14$ (values quoted in the notebook). Every extra qubit multiplies the memory by 4.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $131$ kB $= 16\cdot2^{13}$ bytes is the memory of a 13-qubit \emph{state vector}, not a density matrix.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $268$ MB $= 16\cdot4^{12}$ is the 12-qubit value.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $4.29$ GB $= 16\cdot4^{14}$ is the 14-qubit value.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Each qubit multiplies density-matrix memory by 4.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{49}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{What \texttt{stim} can simulate}
Which simulation can the stabilizer target \texttt{stim} perform \emph{correctly}?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] a GHZ circuit with amplitude-damping noise
\item[\optlabel{B}] a GHZ circuit followed by a $T$ gate, with bit-flip noise
\item[\correctlabel{C}] a GHZ circuit ($H$, CNOT) with depolarizing noise after every gate
\item[\optlabel{D}] the notebook's mirror circuit with random $R_Y$, $R_Z$ rotations and depolarizing noise
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} a GHZ circuit ($H$, CNOT) with depolarizing noise after every gate

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Gottesman--Knill theorem.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Clifford gates + Pauli channels + Pauli measurements: polynomial simulation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The stabilizer formalism (Gottesman--Knill) efficiently simulates Clifford circuits ($H$, $S$, CNOT, Paulis, measurement) with \emph{Pauli} noise, which
maps stabilizer states to probabilistic mixtures of stabilizer states. Arbitrary rotations and $T$ are non-Clifford; amplitude damping is not a Pauli channel.
The notebook raises an error in those cases instead of silently ignoring the noise.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Amplitude damping is not a mixture of Paulis; \texttt{stim} cannot represent it (the notebook refuses this combination).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The $T$ gate is not a Clifford gate; it maps stabilizer states outside the stabilizer set.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The mirror circuit uses $R_Y$, $R_Z$ with random angles: non-Clifford gates that the stabilizer formalism cannot represent.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} \texttt{stim}: Clifford + Pauli noise only.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{50}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{\texttt{as\_counts\_from\_rho}}
On the density-matrix path the notebook calls \texttt{as\_counts\_from\_rho(rho, n, shots)}. What does this function do?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] it takes the diagonal of $\rho$ and returns it unchanged as counts, without sampling
\item[\correctlabel{B}] it takes the diagonal of the exact noisy $\rho$ as outcome probabilities, reorders the indices so that qubit 0 is written first, and draws \texttt{shots} counts from a multinomial distribution
\item[\optlabel{C}] it measures the density-matrix simulator \texttt{shots} times with \texttt{cudaq.sample}
\item[\optlabel{D}] it rounds every entry of $\rho$ to the nearest multiple of $1/\texttt{shots}$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} it takes the diagonal of the exact noisy $\rho$ as outcome probabilities, reorders the indices so that qubit 0 is written first, and draws \texttt{shots} counts from a multinomial distribution

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Sampling from the exact diagonal of $\rho$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Counts $\sim\mathrm{Multinomial}(S, \operatorname{diag}\rho)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The function clips and normalises \texttt{np.real(np.diag(rho))}, applies \texttt{bit\_reverse\_order} (CUDA-Q stores qubit 0 as the least significant
bit), draws \texttt{counts\_rng.multinomial(shots, probs)} with a seeded NumPy generator, and also returns the exact distribution. Because measurement
probabilities are exactly the diagonal of $\rho$, this is statistically identical to noisy sampling --- and much faster than noisy \texttt{cudaq.sample} on the
density-matrix target in CUDA-Q 0.16 (about 115 s for 10 qubits, according to the README).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] It does sample (\texttt{multinomial}); the exact distribution is returned separately as a second value.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The function never calls \texttt{cudaq.sample}; noisy sampling on the density-matrix target was too slow in CUDA-Q 0.16.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] There is no rounding: counts are random multinomial draws from the exact probabilities.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Exact $\rho$ + multinomial draws = noisy shots, fast.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{51}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Hellinger fidelity and TVD}
The ideal distribution of a 2-qubit circuit is $P(00) = P(11) = 0.5$. The noisy distribution is $Q(00) = Q(11) = 0.45$, $Q(01) = Q(10) = 0.05$. The Hellinger
fidelity $F_H = \big(\sum_x\sqrt{P_xQ_x}\big)^2$ and the total variation distance $\frac12\sum_x|P_x - Q_x|$ are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.900$ and $0.200$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.949$ and $0.100$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.810$ and $0.100$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.900$ and $0.100$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.900$ and $0.100$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Distances between probability distributions.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $F_H = (\sum\sqrt{P_xQ_x})^2$, TVD $= \frac12\sum|P_x - Q_x|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\sum_x\sqrt{P_xQ_x} = 2\sqrt{0.5\times0.45} = 2(0.4743) = 0.9487$; squared: $F_H = 0.900$. Only the two ideal outcomes contribute.
TVD $= \frac12(0.05 + 0.05 + 0.05 + 0.05) = 0.100$. For a balanced two-peak ideal distribution $F_H$ equals the population $Q(00) + Q(11)$ --- which is why the
notebook's Hellinger fidelity and GHZ population columns coincide.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.200$ forgets the factor $\frac12$ in the total variation distance.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.949$ is the Bhattacharyya coefficient $\sum\sqrt{P_xQ_x}$ before squaring.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.810$ squares the result once more ($0.9^2$).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} For a two-peak ideal distribution, $F_H$ = population.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{52}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Parity from $X$-basis counts}
A 2-qubit GHZ state is measured after Hadamards on both qubits ($X$ basis): counts \texttt{\{00: 450, 11: 400, 01: 80, 10: 70\}}. The parity
$\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.40$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.15$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.70$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.85$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.70$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Parity from counts.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\langle X^{\otimes N}\rangle = P(\text{even}) - P(\text{odd})$ in the $X$ basis.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Even parity ($00$, $11$) counts $+1$, odd parity ($01$, $10$) counts $-1$: $\langle XX\rangle = \frac{(450 + 400) - (80 + 70)}{1000} = \frac{850 - 150}{1000} = 0.70$.
This is the notebook's \texttt{parity\_expectation}. The ideal GHZ value is 1; phase and bit errors both lower it.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.40$ subtracts the counts of $11$ from those of $00$ and ignores the odd outcomes.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.15 = 150/1000$ is $P(\text{odd parity})$, one of the two terms, not the difference $P(\text{even}) - P(\text{odd})$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.85$ is $P(\text{even parity})$, not $P(\text{even}) - P(\text{odd})$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Parity = even minus odd.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{53}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Trajectories vs density matrix}
For $N = 20$ qubits, by what factor does the memory of exact density-matrix simulation exceed that of one trajectory (state vector) in the same precision?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$20$ & \optlabel{B}\,about $10^{12}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$2$ & \correctlabel{D}\,about $10^6$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} about $10^6$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Memory of density matrices vs trajectories.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $4^N/2^N = 2^N$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\frac{16\cdot4^{20}}{16\cdot2^{20}} = 2^{20} \approx 1.05\times10^6$. Trajectory (Monte-Carlo wave-function) simulation keeps one $2^N$ state and inserts random
Kraus jumps; averaging many trajectories reproduces $\rho$ statistically. It trades memory for repetitions --- CUDA-Q runs it on GPUs (\texttt{nvidia} target with a
noise model), which was not executed for these materials.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $20 = N$ assumes the memory ratio grows linearly with the number of qubits.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $10^{12} \approx 4^{20}$ is the number of density-matrix entries, not the ratio to the $2^{20}$ state vector.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2$ is the ratio of the bases ($4/2$), not of the sizes $4^N/2^N$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Trajectories trade $2^N$ memory for many repetitions.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{54}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{\texttt{add\_all\_qubit\_channel}}
In \texttt{build\_noise\_model} the line \texttt{model.add\_all\_qubit\_channel("x", two, num\_controls=1)} means
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] the channel \texttt{two} is applied once, at the end of the circuit, to the first two qubits
\item[\optlabel{B}] the channel \texttt{two} replaces the CNOT gate
\item[\optlabel{C}] after every single-qubit \texttt{x} gate, the channel \texttt{two} acts on that qubit and its neighbour
\item[\correctlabel{D}] after every CNOT (an \texttt{x} gate with one control), the two-qubit channel \texttt{two} acts on its control and target qubits
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} after every CNOT (an \texttt{x} gate with one control), the two-qubit channel \texttt{two} acts on its control and target qubits

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} \texttt{NoiseModel.add\_all\_qubit\_channel} semantics.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} (gate name, channel, number of controls) $\to$ channel after every matching gate on its qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \texttt{add\_all\_qubit\_channel(name, channel, num\_controls)} attaches a channel to every occurrence of the named gate with that number of controls, on all qubits it
acts on. Plain \texttt{x} gates (no control) get the single-qubit channel \texttt{one} from the loop over \texttt{("h", "x", "ry", "rz")}. The channel is applied
\emph{in addition to}, and after, the ideal gate.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] The channel is attached to every gate occurrence of that type, not applied once at the end.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The ideal CNOT is kept; the channel is applied after it.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Plain \texttt{x} gates (no controls) get the single-qubit channel \texttt{one}; \texttt{num\_controls=1} restricts this line to CNOTs.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} \texttt{num\_controls=1} selects CNOTs.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

Match each CUDA-Q simulation target (List-I) with its property for noisy simulation (List-II).

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Noise-capable CUDA-Q targets.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} stabilizer: poly; trajectory: $16\cdot2^N$; density matrix: $16\cdot4^N$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item \texttt{stim}: the default on a CPU for GHZ with Pauli noise (recorded run) (3);
\item \texttt{density-matrix-cpu}: exact but $4^N$ (4);
\item \texttt{nvidia} + noise model: trajectory method, selected automatically when a GPU is visible (1);

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{56}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Figures of merit}
Match each figure of merit of the notebook (List-I) with what it is sensitive to or requires (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $Z$-basis GHZ population & \textbf{(1)} & needs the full density matrix; also the off-diagonal (coherence) elements \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $X$-basis parity $\langle X^{\otimes N}\rangle$ & \textbf{(2)} & bit flips (errors that change computational-basis outcomes) \\
\textbf{(R)} & state fidelity $\braket{\psi|\rho|\psi}$ & \textbf{(3)} & phase errors, which are invisible in the $Z$ basis \\
\textbf{(S)} & purity $\operatorname{Tr}\rho^2$ & \textbf{(4)} & mixedness of the state, whatever the target \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$4, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$3, S$\to$4 \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$4 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$4
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$4

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} What each figure of merit can detect.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $F_{\mathrm{GHZ}} = \frac12(\rho_{00} + \rho_{dd}) + \operatorname{Re}\rho_{0d}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item population: only diagonal elements; drops with bit flips (2);
\item $X$ parity: $Z$ errors flip its sign (3);
\item state fidelity: for GHZ $F = \frac12(\rho_{0,0} + \rho_{d,d} + 2\operatorname{Re}\rho_{0,d})$ --- needs the coherence $\rho_{0\cdots0,1\cdots1}$, available only on the density-matrix path (1);
\item purity: 1 for pure states, $2^{-N}$ for the maximally mixed state; independent of the target (4).
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$4.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] R$\to$4, S$\to$1 swaps fidelity and purity: purity needs no target state, fidelity does.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$3: the parity is estimated from measured counts, without the density matrix; the fidelity needs $\rho$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] P$\to$3, Q$\to$2 swaps the bases: phase errors are seen by the $X$-basis parity, bit flips by the $Z$-basis population.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Population sees bit flips, parity sees phase flips, fidelity needs $\rho$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{57}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{$(1-p)^G$: bound, not exact value}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} For depolarizing noise, the GHZ state fidelity $\braket{\mathrm{GHZ}|\rho|\mathrm{GHZ}}$ is \emph{exactly} equal to the
no-error probability $(1 - p)^G$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} For Pauli noise, a run without any error produces the ideal state, and no error occurs with probability $(1 - p)^G$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} A is false, but R is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Lower bound vs exact value of the fidelity under Pauli noise.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Pauli channel $= (1-p)\,\mathrm{id} + p\,(\text{Pauli errors})$; $F \ge (1-p)^G$; $Z_iZ_j\ket{\mathrm{GHZ}} = \ket{\mathrm{GHZ}}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true}: a Pauli channel is a mixture ``ideal with probability $1 - p$, Pauli error otherwise''; the error-free branch alone contributes
$(1-p)^G$ to the fidelity, which makes $(1-p)^G$ a \emph{lower bound}. \textbf{A is false}: some error branches also leave the GHZ state unchanged ---
e.g.\ $Z\otimes Z$ after a CNOT ($ZZ\ket{\mathrm{GHZ}} = \ket{\mathrm{GHZ}}$) --- so the fidelity is strictly larger. The lecture's 6-qubit density-matrix run gives
$F = 0.9492$ at $p = 0.01$, while $(0.99)^6 = 0.9415$. (For non-Pauli noise such as amplitude damping the notebook does not claim the bound at all.) Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] requires A to be true, but errors that leave the GHZ state invariant add to the fidelity, so $F > (1-p)^G$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] also requires A to be true (with R not explaining it); A is false because the bound is not tight.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] requires R to be false, but R is exactly the argument that makes $(1-p)^G$ a lower bound.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $(1-p)^G$ is a lower bound for Pauli noise, not the fidelity itself.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{58}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Density-matrix path in CUDA-Q 0.16}
\textbf{Statement I:} In CUDA-Q 0.16 the density-matrix path of the notebook calls \texttt{set\_noise} before \texttt{get\_state},
because \texttt{get\_state} has no \texttt{noise\_model} argument.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} The density-matrix method needs $16\cdot4^N$ bytes, so $N = 14$ needs about $4.3$ GB.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Statement I and Statement II are true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The notebook's density-matrix path in CUDA-Q 0.16.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $16\cdot4^{14} = 4.29\times10^9$ B.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true}: the notebook says so in a comment and uses \texttt{set\_noise} / \texttt{unset\_noise} in a \texttt{try/finally} block (with a deprecation
warning filtered). \textbf{II is true}: $16\times4^{14} = 4.29\times10^9$ bytes. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] requires both statements to be false; both are true.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] requires II to be false, but $16\cdot4^{14} = 4.29\times10^9$ bytes.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] requires I to be false, but the notebook does call \texttt{set\_noise} because \texttt{get\_state} has no noise argument in 0.16.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} \texttt{set\_noise} + \texttt{get\_state}; memory $4^N$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 59 and 60}
The previously recorded run of \texttt{Noise\_Simulation.ipynb} simulates the 15-qubit GHZ circuit ($H$ on qubit 0 and a chain of
14 CNOTs) with depolarizing noise after every gate on the stabilizer target \texttt{stim} (10\,000 shots, seed 42). Part of its table:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{rcccr}\toprule
$p$ & population $P(0\cdots0) + P(1\cdots1)$ & parity $\langle X^{\otimes15}\rangle$ & $(1-p)^G$ & distinct outcomes\\ \midrule
0.01 & 0.8936 & 0.6910 & 0.8601 & 96\\
0.1 & 0.3232 & 0.0160 & 0.2059 & 1165\\ \bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{59}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Recorded run: leaked probability}
The probability mass found \emph{outside} the two ideal GHZ outcomes at $p = 0.01$ and at $p = 0.1$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.1399$ and $0.7941$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.1064$ and $0.6768$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.3090$ and $0.9840$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.8936$ and $0.3232$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.1064$ and $0.6768$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Leaked probability vs error probability.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} leak $= 1 - $ population; $P(\text{some error}) = 1 - (1-p)^G$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} It is $1 - \text{population}$: $1 - 0.8936 = 0.1064$ and $1 - 0.3232 = 0.6768$ (this also equals the total variation distance to the ideal distribution
for a balanced population). $1 - (1-p)^G$ ($0.1399$, $0.7941$) is the probability that \emph{some} error occurred --- larger, because many errors (e.g.\ $Z$ errors) do
not move probability out of the two peaks. $1 - $ parity measures phase damage.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1 - (1-p)^G$ is the probability that \emph{some} error occurred; many errors ($Z$-type) do not move probability out of the two peaks.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $1 - $ parity measures the phase damage seen in the $X$ basis, not the leaked $Z$-basis probability.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.8936$ and $0.3232$ are the populations themselves, i.e.\ the mass \emph{inside} the peaks.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Not every error leaves the ideal outcomes.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{60}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Recorded run: population vs parity}
Why is the population at $p = 0.01$ ($0.8936$) \emph{larger} than $(1 - p)^G = 0.8601$, while the parity ($0.6910$) is smaller?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $(1-p)^G$ is an upper bound on the population, so the population must lie below it --- the table contains a mistake
\item[\correctlabel{B}] $(1-p)^G$ counts every error, but $Z$-type errors leave the $Z$-basis population intact; the parity is also sensitive to those phase errors (and to Hadamard noise in the $X$-basis circuit)
\item[\optlabel{C}] the stabilizer simulator under-reports errors because it cannot simulate depolarizing noise
\item[\optlabel{D}] 10\,000 shots are too few: with more shots the population would fall to exactly $0.8601$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $(1-p)^G$ counts every error, but $Z$-type errors leave the $Z$-basis population intact; the parity is also sensitive to those phase errors (and to Hadamard noise in the $X$-basis circuit)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Interpreting population, parity and bound together.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Pauli noise: $F \ge (1-p)^G$; $Z$ errors invisible to $Z$-basis populations.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $(1-p)^G$ is the weight of the error-free branch, a \emph{lower} bound for Pauli noise. Among the depolarizing errors, $Z$-type errors (e.g.\ $Z$ on one qubit, or $ZZ$ after a CNOT) keep the outcome in $\{0\cdots0, 1\cdots1\}$ --- so does an $X$ error on qubit 0 right after the Hadamard, which the CNOT chain copies to every qubit ---
so the population exceeds the bound. The parity measurement
needs extra Hadamards (also noisy), and $Z$-type errors flip its sign, so it is the more demanding test. The statistical error at 10\,000 shots is only
$\sqrt{0.89\cdot0.11/10^4} \approx 0.003$; \texttt{stim} simulates Pauli channels exactly.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $(1-p)^G$ is a lower bound, not an upper one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] \texttt{stim} simulates Pauli (incl.\ depolarizing) noise exactly.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Shot noise is about $\pm0.003$, far below the difference.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Use several figures of merit; each sees different errors.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION D \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Advanced Noise Analysis and Implementation \hfill Q.61--80\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{61}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Process vs average gate fidelity}
For a single-qubit depolarizing channel (CUDA-Q convention: Kraus operators $\sqrt{1-p}\,I$, $\sqrt{p/3}\,X, Y, Z$) the process (entanglement) fidelity is
$F_{\text{pro}} = 1 - p$. Using $F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{dF_{\text{pro}} + 1}{d + 1}$, the average gate fidelity for $p = 0.003$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.9980$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.9990$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.9970$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.99775$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.9980$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Process vs average gate fidelity.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{dF_{\text{pro}} + 1}{d + 1}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $d = 2$: $F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2(1 - p) + 1}{3} = 1 - \frac{2p}{3} = 1 - 0.002 = 0.9980$; the average gate infidelity (``error rate'') is $r = 0.002$.
$F_{\text{pro}} = 0.997$ itself is lower because it does not average over input states. $1 - \frac{3p}{4}$ mixes up the $\lambda = \frac{4p}{3}$ convention.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.9990 = 1 - \frac p3$ counts only one of the three Pauli errors.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.9970 = 1 - p$ is the process (entanglement) fidelity, which does not average over input states.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.99775 = 1 - \frac{3p}{4}$ uses the convention $\rho \mapsto (1-p)\rho + p\frac I2$, not CUDA-Q's.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Single-qubit depolarizing: $r = \frac{2p}{3}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{62}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Randomized benchmarking}
Single-qubit randomized benchmarking fits the survival probability to $A\alpha^m + B$ ($m$ = sequence length) and finds $\alpha = 0.99$. The error per Clifford
$r = \frac{(d - 1)(1 - \alpha)}{d}$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.010$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.0067$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.0025$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.005$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.005$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Randomized benchmarking decay.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $r = \frac{(d-1)(1-\alpha)}{d}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $d = 2$: $r = \frac{1\cdot(1 - 0.99)}{2} = 0.005$. RB is robust to state-preparation and measurement errors (absorbed in $A$, $B$) and reports an
\emph{average} error per gate under twirled (effectively depolarizing) noise. $1 - \alpha = 0.01$ forgets the factor $\frac{d-1}{d}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.010 = 1 - \alpha$ forgets the factor $\frac{d-1}{d} = \frac12$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.0067 = \frac23(1 - \alpha)$ uses $d = 3$ (a qutrit).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.0025 = \frac14(1-\alpha)$ divides by $d^2 = 4$ instead of using $\frac{d-1}{d}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} RB measures average error per gate, robust to SPAM.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{63}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Linear ZNE}
Zero-noise extrapolation measures $E(1) = 0.80$ at the native noise and $E(2) = 0.64$ at doubled noise. The \emph{linear} extrapolation to $\lambda = 0$ gives
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.88$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.00$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.80$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.96$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.96$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Linear zero-noise extrapolation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E(0) = 2E(1) - E(2)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Line through $(1, 0.80)$ and $(2, 0.64)$: slope $-0.16$, so $E(0) = 0.80 + 0.16 = 0.96$ (formula $2E(1) - E(2)$).
An exponential model $E = ae^{-b\lambda}$ would give $E(1)^2/E(2) = 1.00$: the result depends on the assumed model --- ZNE is a biased estimator.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.88$ interpolates to $\lambda = 1.5$ instead of extrapolating to $\lambda = 0$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.00 = E(1)^2/E(2)$ is the exponential extrapolation, a different model from the requested linear one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.80$ is the unmitigated value at $\lambda = 1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} ZNE result depends on the extrapolation model.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{64}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Richardson ZNE}
ZNE with three noise levels gives $E(1) = 0.80$, $E(2) = 0.65$, $E(3) = 0.53$. The quadratic (Richardson) extrapolation $E(0) = 3E(1) - 3E(2) + E(3)$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.95$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.985$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.98$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.53$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.98$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Richardson extrapolation with three points.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E(0) = 3E(1) - 3E(2) + E(3)$ for $\lambda = 1, 2, 3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $3(0.80) - 3(0.65) + 0.53 = 2.40 - 1.95 + 0.53 = 0.98$. \emph{Check}: the parabola through the three points has second difference
$0.53 - 2(0.65) + 0.80 = 0.03$, so $E(\lambda) = 0.98 - 0.195\lambda + 0.015\lambda^2$. The linear estimate from the first two points is $0.95$; an exponential fit through $\lambda = 1, 2$ gives $0.8^2/0.65 = 0.985$.
The coefficients $(3, -3, 1)$ amplify the statistical errors: $\sqrt{9 + 9 + 1} \approx 4.4$ times the error of one point.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.95 = 2E(1) - E(2)$ is the two-point linear estimate, not the three-point Richardson one.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.985 = E(1)^2/E(2)$ is a two-point exponential fit, not the quadratic Richardson estimate.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.53 = E(3)$ is the most noisy measurement, not an extrapolation.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Higher-order extrapolation: less bias, more variance.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{65}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Gate folding scale factor}
A circuit has 10 gates of equal error. To amplify noise, 4 of them are ``folded'' ($G \to GG^\dagger G$), the others are left unchanged. Assuming the noise grows with
the number of gates, the effective noise scale factor is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$2.2$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.4$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$1.8$ & \optlabel{D}\,$3.0$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $1.8$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Noise amplification by gate folding.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda = \frac{\text{gates after folding}}{\text{original gates}}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each folded gate becomes 3 gates: $4\times3 + 6\times1 = 18$ gates instead of 10, so $\lambda = 18/10 = 1.8$. Folding all gates gives $\lambda = 3$.
Folding keeps the ideal unitary unchanged ($GG^\dagger G = G$) while multiplying the noise --- the hardware analogue of the lecture's ``scale $p$'' experiment.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $2.2 = 22/10$ counts three extra gates per fold.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.4 = 14/10$ counts one extra gate per fold; $GG^\dagger G$ adds two.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $3.0$ assumes all ten gates are folded ($30/10$); only four are folded here.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $GG^\dagger G$ triples the noise of $G$ without changing its action.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{66}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Readout mitigation}
Readout calibration of one qubit gives $P(\text{read }0|0) = 0.98$ and $P(\text{read }0|1) = 0.05$. An experiment reads $0$ with frequency $0.60$. The mitigated
probability of the true state $\ket0$ is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.604$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.591$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.600$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.612$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.591$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Inverting a confusion matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathbf q = A\mathbf p \Rightarrow \mathbf p = A^{-1}\mathbf q$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Solve $\begin{psmallmatrix}0.98 & 0.05\\ 0.02 & 0.95\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}p_0\\ p_1\end{psmallmatrix} = \begin{psmallmatrix}0.60\\ 0.40\end{psmallmatrix}$ with
$p_0 + p_1 = 1$: $0.98p_0 + 0.05(1 - p_0) = 0.60 \Rightarrow 0.93p_0 = 0.55 \Rightarrow p_0 = 0.5914$. $0.6/0.98 = 0.612$ ignores the $1\to0$ errors;
$0.604$ comes from the transposed confusion matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.604$ results from the transposed confusion matrix ($0.98p_0 + 0.02p_1 = 0.60$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.600$ is the raw (unmitigated) frequency; it still contains the misassigned $\ket1$ shots.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.612 = 0.60/0.98$ corrects only the $0 \to 1$ errors and ignores the $1 \to 0$ errors.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Columns of $A$ = true states, rows = read outcomes.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{67}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Limits of readout mitigation}
Which statement about readout-error mitigation by inverting the calibrated confusion matrix $A$ is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] it reduces the number of shots needed, because $A^{-1}$ removes the shot noise
\item[\optlabel{B}] it requires quantum error correction to estimate $A$
\item[\optlabel{C}] it also corrects gate errors that happened before the measurement
\item[\correctlabel{D}] $A^{-1}\mathbf q$ can contain small negative ``quasi-probabilities'', and the full $2^N\times2^N$ matrix becomes impractical for many qubits
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $A^{-1}\mathbf q$ can contain small negative ``quasi-probabilities'', and the full $2^N\times2^N$ matrix becomes impractical for many qubits

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Limits of readout mitigation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathbf p = A^{-1}\mathbf q$; variance grows with $\|A^{-1}\|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Inversion only undoes the classical misassignment of outcomes. Shot noise in $\mathbf q$ propagates (and is amplified) through $A^{-1}$, which can produce slightly
negative entries --- the lecture's 3-qubit example gave a minimum of $-0.0009$; they are usually clipped or handled by constrained least squares. $A$ is measured
by preparing and reading basis states; for many qubits one assumes tensor-product or correlated sparse models instead of the full $4^N$-entry matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Inversion amplifies the shot noise ($A^{-1}$ has norm $> 1$); it cannot reduce the number of shots needed.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $A$ is estimated by preparing basis states and measuring them --- no error correction is involved.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Errors in the gates before the measurement change the state; the confusion matrix only models the classical readout step.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Readout mitigation is post-processing; quasi-probabilities can be negative.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{68}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Ramsey vs Hahn echo}
A qubit in $\ket+$ idles for $t$ with a random but \emph{static} detuning $\delta \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$, $\sigma = 1$ rad/$\mu$s, so it acquires the phase $\delta t$. At
$t = 2\,\mu$s the average coherence $\langle X\rangle$ without and with a Hahn echo ($X$ pulse at $t/2$ and again at the end) is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.135$ and $0.135$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.368$ and $1.0$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.607$ and $1.0$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.135$ and $1.0$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.135$ and $1.0$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Ramsey decay vs spin echo for static noise.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathbb E\cos(\delta t) = e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$; $XR_Z(a)X = R_Z(-a)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Without echo: $\langle X\rangle = \mathbb E\cos(\delta t) = e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2} = e^{-2} = 0.135$ (Gaussian characteristic function).
With echo: $R_Z(\varphi/2)\,X\,R_Z(\varphi/2) = X$ because $XR_Z(a)X = R_Z(-a)$; the two halves cancel for \emph{every} static $\delta$, so $\langle X\rangle = 1$.
($e^{-1} = 0.368$ uses $e^{-\sigma^2t^2/4}$; $0.607 = e^{-1/2}$ uses $t = 1$.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.135$ with echo ignores that the echo cancels a static phase exactly.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.368 = e^{-1}$ uses $e^{-\sigma^2t^2/4}$; the Gaussian average is $\mathbb E\cos(\delta t) = e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.607 = e^{-1/2}$ is the free decay at $t = 1\,\mu$s, not $2\,\mu$s.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Echoes cancel slow noise.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{69}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{DD and Markovian noise}
Now the dephasing is Markovian: an independent phase-flip channel with $p = 0.02$ acts after each of 20 idle steps on $\ket+$. With a Hahn echo inserted at step 10,
$\langle X\rangle$ at the end is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.000$ \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$0.442$, the same as without echo & \optlabel{D}\,$0.668$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.442$, the same as without echo

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Markovian noise and dynamical decoupling.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\langle X\rangle = (1-2p)^n$; $X$ commutes with the phase-flip channel.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each step multiplies $\langle X\rangle$ by $1 - 2p = 0.96$: $0.96^{20} = 0.442$. The $X$ pulses commute with the phase-flip channel up to the sign that the second
$X$ undoes, and independent random flips in the two halves do not cancel. The lecture's density-matrix simulation gives $0.4420$ both with and without echo:
dynamical decoupling only fights noise that is slow (correlated in time) compared with the pulse spacing.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0$: the coherence decays to $0.96^{20} = 0.44$, it does not vanish.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.000$ assumes the echo cancels the phase flips, but independent random flips in the two halves do not cancel.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.668 = 0.98^{20}$ uses $1 - p$ instead of $1 - 2p$ per step.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} DD does not help against white (uncorrelated) noise.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{70}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{3-qubit bit-flip code}
In the 3-qubit bit-flip code each qubit flips independently with probability $p$, and encoding and correction are perfect. The logical error probability at $p = 0.1$, and
the value of $p$ above which encoding is worse than an unencoded qubit, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.028$ and $p = 0.5$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.010$ and $p = 0.5$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.028$ and $p = 1/3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.030$ and $p = 0.5$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.028$ and $p = 0.5$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Repetition code and break-even.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P_L = 3p^2 - 2p^3$; $P_L < p \Leftrightarrow p < \frac12$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Majority vote fails when 2 or 3 qubits flip: $P_L = 3p^2(1-p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3 = 0.03 - 0.002 = 0.028$ (the lecture's CUDA-Q density-matrix simulation
reproduces this formula to $10^{-16}$). $P_L < p \Leftrightarrow 3p - 2p^2 < 1 \Leftrightarrow (2p - 1)(p - 1) > 0 \Leftrightarrow p < \frac12$. $3p^2 = 0.030$ drops the
$-2p^3$ term.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.010 = p^2$ forgets the three ways of choosing two flipped qubits.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Break-even at $p = \frac13$ is wrong: $3p^2 - 2p^3 < p \Leftrightarrow p < \frac12$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.030 = 3p^2$ drops the $-2p^3$ term (the probability of three flips is counted three times).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Encoding helps below a threshold.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{71}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Surface-code scaling}
A surface-code memory has logical error rate $p_L \approx A(p/p_{\text{th}})^{(d+1)/2}$ for code distance $d$. With $p/p_{\text{th}} = 0.1$, increasing the distance from
$d = 3$ to $d = 5$ reduces $p_L$ by a factor of
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,none: $p_L$ increases by a factor of 10 & \correctlabel{B}\,$10$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$2$ & \optlabel{D}\,$100$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $10$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Below-threshold scaling of surface codes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $p_L \propto (p/p_{\text{th}})^{(d+1)/2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The exponent goes from $2$ to $3$: $p_L$ is multiplied by $(p/p_{\text{th}})^{1} = 0.1$, i.e.\ reduced by a factor of 10. Below threshold ($p < p_{\text{th}}$) larger
codes suppress errors exponentially in $d$; above threshold they make things worse. QEC needs many physical qubits and fast feedback --- it is not
implemented in this repository.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Below threshold ($p < p_{\text{th}}$) larger codes \emph{reduce} $p_L$; it increases only above threshold.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2$ ignores the power law; the reduction factor is $(p/p_{\text{th}})^{-1} = 10$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $100$ corresponds to an exponent increase of 2; going from $d = 3$ to $d = 5$ raises $\frac{d+1}{2}$ from 2 to 3, by 1.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Each $+2$ in distance multiplies $p_L$ by $p/p_{\text{th}}$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{72}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Coherent vs stochastic accumulation}
Each of $n = 60$ idle gates over-rotates coherently by $\varepsilon = 0.05$ rad about $x$. Compare with a stochastic bit flip of the same per-gate error probability
$p = \sin^2(\varepsilon/2)$. Starting from $\ket0$, the probabilities of finding $1$ after 60 gates are approximately
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.995$ (coherent) and $0.036$ (stochastic) & \optlabel{B}\,$0.0375$ and $0.036$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.995$ and $0.995$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.036$ and $0.036$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.995$ (coherent) and $0.036$ (stochastic)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Coherent vs stochastic accumulation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Coherent $\sin^2(n\varepsilon/2)$; stochastic $\frac12[1 - (1-2p)^n]$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Coherent: the rotations add up, $R_X(\varepsilon)^{60} = R_X(3)$: $P(1) = \sin^2(1.5) = 0.995$. Stochastic: $p = \sin^2(0.025) = 6.25\times10^{-4}$ per gate and
$P(1) = \frac12[1 - (1 - 2p)^{60}] = \frac12(1 - 0.9278) = 0.036 \approx np$. Coherent errors grow like $n^2\varepsilon^2$ (amplitudes add), stochastic ones like $np$.
Both values were computed with CUDA-Q for the lecture. Randomized compiling/Pauli twirling turns the former into the latter.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $np = 0.0375$ is the stochastic estimate, not the coherent one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Stochastic errors grow linearly, not like coherent ones.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Coherent errors do not add like probabilities.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Coherent errors can be far worse than their per-gate fidelity suggests.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{73}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Pauli twirling}
Which statement about Pauli twirling (randomized compiling) is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] it removes all errors, so the circuit becomes noiseless
\item[\correctlabel{B}] averaging a gate over random Pauli frames that cancel ideally turns its coherent error into a stochastic Pauli channel with the same average fidelity
\item[\optlabel{C}] it requires a density-matrix simulator and cannot be done on hardware
\item[\optlabel{D}] it converts stochastic Pauli noise into coherent errors to make them easier to correct
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} averaging a gate over random Pauli frames that cancel ideally turns its coherent error into a stochastic Pauli channel with the same average fidelity

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli twirling / randomized compiling.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathcal E_{\text{twirl}}(\rho) = \frac1{|\mathcal P|}\sum_PP^\dagger\mathcal E(P\rho P^\dagger)P$ is a Pauli channel.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Inserting random Paulis $P$ before a gate and the compensating $P'$ after it leaves the ideal circuit unchanged; averaged over many random compilations the
effective channel is diagonal in the Pauli basis --- a Pauli (stochastic) channel. This prevents the quadratic, worst-case accumulation of coherent errors and makes
noise models such as those of the notebook (Pauli channels) realistic. It does not reduce the average error itself.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Twirling reshapes the error into a Pauli channel but keeps its average fidelity; the circuit is not noiseless.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Randomized compiling is a compilation technique used on hardware; it needs no simulator.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Twirling works in the opposite direction: it turns coherent errors into stochastic Pauli noise.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Twirling makes noise stochastic, and Pauli-noise simulation realistic.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}

\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Notebook: \texttt{auto} method choice}
The noise notebook runs on a CPU (no GPU visible) with the settings\\
\hspace*{1em}\texttt{CIRCUIT = "ghz"},\ \ \texttt{NOISE\_MODEL = "amplitude\_damping"},\ \ \texttt{SIMULATION\_METHOD = "auto"}.\\
Which method does it choose?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] \texttt{stabilizer} (target \texttt{stim})
\item[\optlabel{B}] \texttt{trajectory} (target \texttt{nvidia})
\item[\optlabel{C}] \texttt{statevector} (target \texttt{qpp-cpu})
\item[\correctlabel{D}] \texttt{density\_matrix} (target \texttt{density-matrix-cpu})
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} \texttt{density\_matrix} (target \texttt{density-matrix-cpu})

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} The notebook's \texttt{auto} method rule.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} GPU $\to$ trajectory; CPU + GHZ + Pauli $\to$ stabilizer; else density matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The \texttt{"auto"} rule: GPU visible $\to$ \texttt{trajectory}; otherwise \texttt{stabilizer} only for GHZ \emph{with Pauli noise}; otherwise \texttt{density\_matrix}.
Amplitude damping is not a Pauli channel, so \texttt{stim} would silently ignore it --- the notebook even raises an error if \texttt{stabilizer} is forced with it.
\texttt{statevector} is refused because noiseless simulators ignore noise models.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}

\item[\textbf{(B)}] \texttt{trajectory} is chosen only when a GPU is visible; this case is a CPU.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The notebook refuses \texttt{statevector}: noiseless simulators ignore noise models.

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{75}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Mitigation, DD, QEC}
Match each technique (List-I) with its description (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & zero-noise extrapolation & \textbf{(1)} & invert a calibrated confusion matrix applied to the measured distribution \\
\textbf{(Q)} & readout-error mitigation & \textbf{(2)} & run the circuit at amplified noise levels and extrapolate the observable to zero noise \\
\textbf{(R)} & dynamical decoupling & \textbf{(3)} & encode logical qubits redundantly, measure syndromes and correct; needs physical errors below a threshold \\
\textbf{(S)} & quantum error correction & \textbf{(4)} & apply pulse sequences during idle periods to refocus slow (quasi-static) dephasing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$1, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$3 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$3, S$\to$4 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Mitigation vs correction vs decoupling.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} ZNE: extrapolate $E(\lambda)$; readout: $A^{-1}\mathbf q$; DD: refocus; QEC: encode + syndromes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item ZNE: an \emph{estimator} for expectation values, post-processing (2);
\item readout mitigation: classical post-processing of counts (1);
\item DD: changes the physical evolution during idling (4);
\item QEC: protects the quantum state itself during the computation (3).
\end{itemize}
Only QEC corrects errors on the quantum state; ZNE and readout mitigation correct estimates; noise \emph{simulation} does neither. Hence P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$3.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] P$\to$1, Q$\to$2 swaps ZNE and readout mitigation.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] R$\to$3, S$\to$4 swaps dynamical decoupling (pulses during idling) and error correction (encoding and syndromes).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Q$\to$4, R$\to$1 swaps readout mitigation (classical post-processing) and dynamical decoupling (physical pulses).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Only QEC protects the state itself.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{76}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Error taxonomy}
Match each physical cause (List-I) with its category (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & a pulse amplitude 1\,\% too large on every $X$ gate & \textbf{(1)} & decoherence (non-unital, $T_1$) \\
\textbf{(Q)} & a random Pauli error after each gate & \textbf{(2)} & classical measurement (readout) error \\
\textbf{(R)} & energy loss of $\ket1$ to the environment & \textbf{(3)} & coherent error (unitary, systematic) \\
\textbf{(S)} & the discriminator assigns some $\ket1$ shots to outcome 0 & \textbf{(4)} & stochastic (incoherent) gate noise \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Error taxonomy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} coherent $U_\varepsilon$; stochastic $\sum p_kP_k\cdot P_k$; decoherence $T_1, T_2$; readout $A$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item over-rotation: the same unitary error every time (3);
\item random Pauli: a probabilistic mixture --- the notebook's model (4);
\item energy loss: amplitude damping, $T_1$ (1);
\item misassignment: acts on the classical outcome after the quantum measurement (2).
\end{itemize}
Hence P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$3 swaps coherent and stochastic errors: the miscalibration is the same every time (coherent).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] R$\to$2, S$\to$1 swaps decoherence (quantum) and misassignment (classical readout).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps random Pauli errors (stochastic) and energy loss (amplitude damping, $T_1$).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Different error types need different remedies.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{77}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Cost and nature of ZNE}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} Zero-noise extrapolation increases the number of circuit executions needed to reach a given statistical precision.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} ZNE corrects errors on the quantum state during the computation, in the same way as quantum error correction.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} A is true, but R is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Cost and nature of ZNE.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\operatorname{Var}[E_0] = \sum_k\gamma_k^2\operatorname{Var}[E(\lambda_k)]$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true}: several noise levels must be run, and extrapolation coefficients (e.g.\ $3, -3, 1$) amplify the statistical error, so more shots are needed for the same
error bar. \textbf{R is false}: ZNE never touches the quantum state; it post-processes noisy expectation values and returns a (biased) estimate. Only QEC protects the
state, and it can do so for arbitrary-length computations. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] requires R to be true; ZNE does not act on the state.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] also requires R to be true (with R not explaining A); R is false because ZNE never acts on the state.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] requires A to be false, but extra noise levels and amplified variance always cost extra shots.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Mitigation trades shots for bias reduction; it does not fix the state.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\textbf{Statement II:} The recorded results of \texttt{Noise\_Simulation.ipynb} were obtained on a physical quantum processor.

\item[\correctlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false

\textbf{II is false}: the recorded run used the \texttt{stim} simulator on a CPU (no GPU visible); the notebook even refuses \texttt{BACKEND = "hardware"}, because noise
models are a simulator feature. Answer: (B).

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 79 and 80}
For the lecture (illustrative experiment, not part of the notebook), zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) was applied to the parity
$\langle X^{\otimes4}\rangle$ of a 4-qubit GHZ state. The circuit was simulated exactly on \texttt{density-matrix-cpu} with the notebook's
depolarizing noise model at the scaled probability $p = 0.01\lambda$ (noise scale factor $\lambda$). The ideal value is $1$.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{cccc}\toprule $\lambda$ & 1 & 2 & 3\\ \midrule $\langle X^{\otimes4}\rangle$ & 0.9055 & 0.8189 & 0.7396\\ \bottomrule\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{79}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{ZNE extrapolation values}
The linear extrapolation from $\lambda = 1, 2$ and the Richardson (quadratic) extrapolation from $\lambda = 1, 2, 3$ give
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$0.9921$ and $0.9994$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0.9055$ and $0.9921$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.9921$ and $1.0021$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.9872$ and $0.9994$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $0.9921$ and $0.9994$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Applying linear and Richardson extrapolation to data.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $2E_1 - E_2$; $3E_1 - 3E_2 + E_3$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Linear: $2E(1) - E(2) = 1.8110 - 0.8189 = 0.9921$. Richardson: $3E(1) - 3E(2) + E(3) = 2.7165 - 2.4567 + 0.7396 = 0.9994$.
Both reduce the error of the raw value $0.9055$ ($9.5\,\%$) to below $1\,\%$. $1.0021$ is the exponential fit, which overshoots the physical maximum.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $0.9055$ is the raw value at $\lambda = 1$, not an extrapolation; $0.9921$ is the linear (not the Richardson) estimate.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $1.0021$ is the exponential fit, which overshoots the physical maximum of a parity.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.9872$ is the least-squares straight line through all three points, a different (and here worse) linear estimator than the two-point formula.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Extrapolation removes most of the bias in this example.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{80}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Interpreting ZNE}
Which conclusion about this ZNE experiment is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] on hardware the same result is obtained without scaling the noise, since $\lambda$ is a software parameter
\item[\optlabel{B}] ZNE has corrected the GHZ state itself, so a subsequent circuit could use the improved state
\item[\correctlabel{C}] the extrapolated values depend on the fitted model (an exponential fit gives $1.0021 > 1$, unphysical) and, with shot noise, would carry larger error bars than the raw value
\item[\optlabel{D}] because the exact density matrix was used, ZNE is no longer needed: the raw value $0.9055$ is already the ideal one
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} the extrapolated values depend on the fitted model (an exponential fit gives $1.0021 > 1$, unphysical) and, with shot noise, would carry larger error bars than the raw value

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Interpreting ZNE results honestly.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} Bias depends on the model; variance amplification $\sqrt{\sum\gamma_k^2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} ZNE estimates an expectation value; the state remains noisy. Different extrapolation models give $0.9921$, $0.9994$, $1.0021$ --- a model-dependent
bias, and $1.0021$ exceeds the allowed range of a parity. Here the inputs were exact; with $S$ shots per point, the Richardson combination would multiply the
statistical error by about $\sqrt{19} \approx 4.4$. On hardware the noise cannot be scaled by changing $p$; it is amplified physically, e.g.\ by gate folding or pulse
stretching.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] On hardware $p$ cannot be set in software; noise must be amplified physically (gate folding, pulse stretching).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] ZNE post-processes expectation values; the GHZ state itself stays noisy and cannot be reused in a better form.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The exact density matrix is still the \emph{noisy} state; $0.9055 \neq 1$ shows the remaining bias.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} ZNE is a model-dependent estimator, not error correction.
\end{solbox}
\qsep
